questions.q: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?
questions.a: A list is mutable (you can add, remove or change items). A tuple is immutable (fixed once created). Tuples are slightly faster, use less memory, and can be used as dictionary keys because they are hashable. Lists cannot be dictionary keys.

questions.q: What does 'is' do and how is it different from '=='?
questions.a: '==' checks whether two values are EQUAL. 'is' checks whether two names point to the very SAME object in memory. [1,2] == [1,2] is True, but [1,2] is [1,2] is False because they are two separate lists. Use 'is' mostly for None: if x is None.

questions.q: Why is b = a dangerous for lists?
questions.a: It does not copy the list. Both a and b point to the same list, so changing one changes the other. Make a copy with b = a[:] or b = a.copy(). For lists inside lists use copy.deepcopy(a).

questions.q: What is the output of print(7 // 2, -7 // 2, 7 % 3, -7 % 3)?
questions.a: 3 -4 1 2. Floor division rounds DOWN toward minus infinity, so -7 // 2 is -4. The remainder always has the same sign as the divisor, so -7 % 3 is 2. This differs from C and Java, so be careful.

questions.q: How do you read n integers from one line in Python?
questions.a:
```
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
```
input() reads the line as text, split() cuts it into pieces, map(int, ...) converts every piece to an integer, and list() collects them.

questions.q: What is a mutable default argument bug?
questions.a:
```
def add(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items
```
The default list is created ONCE when the function is defined, so every call that uses the default shares the same list. The fix is items=None and then 'if items is None: items = []' inside the function.

questions.q: What does print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) show and why?
questions.a: False. Floats are stored in binary, and 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare floats with a tolerance: abs(a - b) < 1e-9, or use math.isclose(a, b).

questions.q: Why does Python have no integer overflow?
questions.a: Python ints are arbitrary precision. When a value exceeds the machine word size, Python stores it as multiple digits. The cost is speed on enormous numbers, but correctness is automatic. This is why problems asking for answers modulo 10^9+7 are still required: the judge wants a small number.

questions.q: Write a function that returns the sum of the digits of a number without converting to a string.
questions.a:
```
def digit_sum(n):
    total = 0
    while n > 0:
        total += n % 10
        n //= 10
    return total
```
n % 10 takes the last digit and n // 10 removes it.

questions.q: Now do the same for negative numbers and for a number given as a string with up to 10^6 digits.
questions.a: For negatives use abs(n) first. For a huge digit string, do not convert to int; loop over the characters: sum(int(ch) for ch in s if ch.isdigit()). O(length) time.

questions.q: Why do online judges give wrong answer for an extra space at the end of a line?
questions.a: Many judges compare output text exactly (some trim trailing whitespace, but you cannot rely on it). The safe habit: print exactly what the format says, use print(*items) for space-separated lines and avoid prompts like 'Enter n:'.

questions.q: Tell me about a bug you found because of an input/format mistake and how you prevented it later.
questions.a: A good answer is a specific story: I misread that the first line was the count, so my list was off by one and the hidden tests failed. I now (1) rewrite the input format in a comment, (2) test the sample in the exact judge format, and (3) always test one empty or minimal case before submitting.

questions.q: Why does Python not make you declare variable types?
questions.a: Python decides the type from the value at run time (dynamic typing). It makes short programs easy to write. The price is that mistakes (like adding a number to text) appear only when that line runs.

questions.q: Why not use input() for very large input?
questions.a: Each input() call has overhead. For 10^5 lines the calls add up. sys.stdin.read().split() reads everything at once and is much faster.

questions.q: Why convert with int() instead of just using the text?
questions.a: Text '5' + '3' joins to '53'. Only numbers can be added. The conversion tells Python what kind of data you mean.

questions.q: Why use a for loop instead of a while loop when counting?
questions.a: A for loop updates the counter for you, so you cannot forget it and create an endless loop. while is for 'repeat until something changes'.

questions.q: Why not name variables a, b, c?
questions.a: Short names hide meaning. total_marks tells the reader (and you, an hour later) what the value is. Good names are a cheap form of documentation.

questions.q: Why should you not print prompts like 'Enter a number' in a coding round?
questions.a: The judge compares your output exactly with the expected output. Extra text makes every test fail even if your logic is correct.

questions.q: What does print(type(5 / 2), type(5 // 2)) print?
questions.a: <class 'float'> <class 'int'>. / always returns a float, // returns an int when both operands are ints.

questions.q: Read a number n and print the sum of the first n natural numbers in one line.
questions.a:
```
n = int(input())
print(n * (n + 1) // 2)
```
Using the formula avoids a loop; // keeps the result an integer.

questions.q: How do you approach a coding problem you have never seen?
questions.a: I go in steps: (1) restate the problem in my own words, (2) note input, output and constraints, (3) work the sample by hand, (4) list edge cases, (5) think of a simple brute-force way and its time cost, (6) improve it with a suitable tool (hash map, sorting, two pointers...), (7) code it, and (8) dry-run it on the sample and an edge case.

questions.q: What do you do if you are stuck?
questions.a: I try a smaller input by hand and look for a pattern, ask what work is being repeated, and think about which data structure fits. If I still have no idea, I write the brute force first - a correct slow solution is better than nothing and often shows where to optimise.

questions.q: Why do constraints matter?
questions.a: They tell you the speed your solution needs. About 10^7 to 10^8 simple operations fit in one second. If n = 10^5 then O(n^2) (10^10 steps) is too slow but O(n log n) is fine.

questions.q: What are edge cases? Give examples.
questions.a: Edge cases are unusual inputs that often break code: an empty list, one element, all elements equal, negative numbers, zero, duplicate values, the largest allowed input, and a target that is missing.

questions.q: Why should you ask clarifying questions in an interview?
questions.a: Problems are deliberately underspecified. Asking about input size, duplicates, sorted or not, negative numbers and expected output on invalid input shows maturity, and the answers often reveal the intended algorithm.

questions.q: You wrote a solution. What do you do before saying 'done'?
questions.a: Dry-run it on the sample, run an empty and single-element input, state the time and space complexity, and mention what I would improve with more time.

questions.q: How do constraints guide your choice of algorithm?
questions.a: n up to about 20 permits exponential search; up to about 500 allows O(n^3); up to a few thousand O(n^2); 10^5 requires O(n log n) or O(n); 10^7 or more needs near O(n) or O(log n) per query.

questions.q: Describe how you handle a task when requirements are unclear.
questions.a: I restate the requirement in my own words, list assumptions and open questions, confirm them with the owner, and start with the smallest useful version while keeping the unclear parts easy to change.

questions.q: What is wrong with testing only the sample input?
questions.a: Samples are usually the easy case. Hidden tests cover boundaries, large inputs, and special values. A solution can pass the sample and fail most tests, so always add your own edge cases.

questions.q: Why write down edge cases before coding?
questions.a: Because after coding you will unconsciously test only inputs your code already handles. Listing them first makes you design for them.

questions.q: Why not start coding as soon as you see a familiar problem?
questions.a: Similar-looking problems often differ in one detail (distinct vs duplicates, sorted vs unsorted, indices vs values). Coding the wrong variant wastes the whole attempt.

questions.q: Why do constraints decide the algorithm?
questions.a: They tell you how many steps you can afford. n = 10^5 allows about n log n steps, so an O(n^2) idea is rejected before you write it.

questions.q: Why dry-run instead of just running the code?
questions.a: Running tells you the result is wrong; dry running shows exactly which line first goes wrong. It also works when no judge or tests are available.

questions.q: Why break a problem into steps?
questions.a: People hold only a few things in mind at once. Small steps fit in memory, are easy to test separately and map to functions.

questions.q: Why not trust the sample test alone?
questions.a: Samples are usually the easy case. Hidden tests include empty input, single values, duplicates, negatives and maximum size.

questions.q: Give an example where a misread requirement caused a bug.
questions.a: A statement said 'positive integers' but the data contained 0, so a division failed. Re-reading constraints and testing zero would have caught it.

questions.q: You finished early. How do you use the remaining time?
questions.a: Re-read the statement against my output format, test boundary inputs, reconsider complexity on the largest input, and clean up variable names.

questions.q: What is recursion and what must every recursive function have?
questions.a: Recursion is a function calling itself on a smaller problem. It must have a base case (stops the calls) and a recursive step that gets closer to the base case. Without them it never ends and Python raises RecursionError.

questions.q: What is the time and space complexity of recursive factorial?
questions.a: Time O(n) because there are n calls. Space O(n) because n frames sit on the call stack at the deepest point. An iterative loop uses O(1) space.

questions.q: How do you avoid RecursionError for deep recursion?
questions.a: Convert the recursion to a loop with your own stack, or raise the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit (use with care), or restructure the algorithm (for example iterative DFS).

questions.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
questions.a: A parameter is the variable name in the function definition. An argument is the real value you pass when calling. In def f(x): x is a parameter; in f(5) the 5 is an argument.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```
def f(n):
    if n == 0:
        return
    print(n)
    f(n - 1)
    print(n)
f(3)
```
questions.a: 3 2 1 1 2 3 (each on its own line). Going down it prints 3, 2, 1; after the base case returns, each pending call prints its own n on the way back up: 1, 2, 3.

questions.q: What is the difference between direct and indirect recursion?
questions.a: Direct: f calls f. Indirect: f calls g and g calls f. Both need base cases to stop.

questions.q: Write a recursive function to reverse a string.
questions.a:
```
def rev(s):
    if len(s) <= 1:
        return s
    return rev(s[1:]) + s[0]
```
Base case: 0 or 1 characters. Recursive step: reverse the rest and put the first character at the end. O(n^2) because slicing copies; an index-based version is O(n).

questions.q: Your recursive solution hits RecursionError for n = 100000. What do you do?
questions.a: Convert it to a loop or use an explicit stack. Raising the limit is risky. If subproblems repeat, convert to bottom-up dynamic programming.

questions.q: Where does recursion appear in everyday software?
questions.a: Directory traversal, parsing JSON/HTML, rendering nested UI components, evaluating expressions, game tree search and divide-and-conquer sorting.

questions.q: Why does recursion need a base case?
questions.a: Without a stopping point the function keeps calling itself until Python raises RecursionError. The base case is the smallest problem you can answer directly.

questions.q: Why not always use recursion since it looks shorter?
questions.a: Each call uses a stack frame and Python limits depth to about 1000. Loops are faster and use constant memory for simple repetition.

questions.q: Why use functions at all?
questions.a: To name a piece of logic, reuse it, test it alone and keep each part small enough to understand.

questions.q: Why does a function return None if you forget return?
questions.a: Python functions always return something; with no return statement the result is None. This is why print(f()) sometimes shows None.

questions.q: Why use default arguments carefully?
questions.a: Defaults are created once. A mutable default like [] is shared between calls, so values from earlier calls leak into later ones.

questions.q: Why is recursion natural for trees but not for summing a list?
questions.a: A tree node is made of smaller trees, so the code mirrors the data. A list can be summed with a simple loop without any stack cost.

questions.q: Write a recursive function that counts down from n to 1.
questions.a:
```
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)
```

questions.q: What does factorial(0) return and why?
questions.a: 1. By definition 0! = 1, and it serves as the base case for the recursion.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of binary search and why?
questions.a: O(log n). Each step throws away half of the remaining items, so the number of steps is how many times you can halve n before reaching 1, which is log2(n).

questions.q: What is the difference between O(n) and O(2n)?
questions.a: No difference in Big-O. Constants are dropped, so O(2n) is O(n). Both grow in a straight line.

questions.q: What is the complexity of two loops, one after the other, each running n times? What if one loop is inside the other?
questions.a: One after the other: O(n) + O(n) = O(n). One inside the other: O(n * n) = O(n^2).

questions.q: What is the worst case of searching a list with 'x in nums'?
questions.a: O(n). In the worst case x is last or missing and Python has to check every element.

questions.q: Is O(n log n) faster than O(n^2)?
questions.a: Yes for large n. For n = 1000: n log n is about 10,000 steps while n^2 is 1,000,000. The gap grows as n grows.

questions.q: What is amortised O(1)?
questions.a: An operation that is occasionally expensive but cheap on average over many calls. list.append is amortised O(1): usually one step, sometimes it copies the list to a bigger memory block, but spread over all appends the average is constant.

questions.q: Why do we drop constants and lower-order terms?
questions.a: Because for large n the dominant term decides the growth, and constants depend on hardware and language. 5n^2 + 100n is O(n^2); the 5 and the 100n become minor as n grows.
O(n^2). The inner loop runs 0 + 1 + ... + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2 times, which is quadratic.

questions.q:
What is the complexity of this?
```
i = n
while i > 0:
    i //= 2
```
questions.a: O(log n). i halves every iteration.

questions.q: Your algorithm is O(n log n) and you have n = 10^6. Is that fine in Python?
questions.a: About 2 x 10^7 basic steps: usually fine if the work per step is small and uses built-ins like sorted(); it may be tight with heavy Python loops. Prefer built-ins and avoid per-step overhead.

questions.q: Why does an O(n^2) feature work in testing and die in production?
questions.a: Test data is small. Growth is invisible at n = 100 but at n = 10^6 the same feature does 10^12 steps. Reasoning about complexity before shipping avoids this.

questions.q: Return True if any two numbers in a list sum to k. Give two solutions and their complexity.
questions.a: Brute force: two nested loops, O(n^2) time, O(1) space. Hash set: for each x check k - x in the set, then add x; O(n) time, O(n) space.

questions.q: Why do we ignore constants in Big-O?
questions.a: Constants depend on the machine and language. For large n the growth shape decides the winner, so 5n and 100n are both 'linear'.

questions.q: Why not just measure seconds?
questions.a: Seconds change with hardware, input and noise. Complexity predicts behaviour before running and compares algorithms fairly.

questions.q: Why usually talk about the worst case?
questions.a: It is a guarantee: no input can be slower. Best case is rarely realistic and average case needs assumptions about the data.

questions.q: Why does O(log n) feel almost free?
questions.a: Doubling the input adds only one step. log2 of a billion is about 30.

questions.q: Why is O(n!) worse than O(2^n)?
questions.a: n! multiplies by a bigger number each step (n, then n-1, ...) while 2^n multiplies by 2 each time. At n = 20, n! is about 2.4 x 10^18 versus 2^20 about 10^6.

questions.q: Why can an O(n^2) algorithm beat O(n log n) for small n?
questions.a: Complexity hides constants and overhead. For tiny inputs a simple loop with small constants can be faster than a clever method with setup cost. Growth wins only at larger n.

questions.q: What is the difference between O, Omega and Theta?
questions.a: O is an upper bound, Omega a lower bound, Theta a tight bound (both). Everyday speech uses O for the tight worst case.
O(n). The inner loop always runs 10 times (a constant), so total steps are 10n.

questions.q: What is the complexity of: for i in range(n): for j in range(i, n): ...?
questions.a: The inside runs n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2 times, which is O(n^2).

questions.q: What is the complexity of: i = 1; while i < n: i *= 2?
questions.a: O(log n). i doubles each time, so it takes log2(n) steps to reach n.

questions.q: How would you reduce the time of checking if a list has duplicates?
questions.a: Brute force compares all pairs in O(n^2). Put elements into a set while scanning; if an element is already in the set you found a duplicate. That is O(n) time and O(n) space.

questions.q: What is the complexity of recursive Fibonacci and how can you improve it?
questions.a: O(2^n) because each call makes two calls and subproblems repeat. Add memoisation (a dictionary or lru_cache) so each value is computed once: O(n) time, O(n) space.

questions.q: Why does appending with s += ch in a loop matter for strings?
questions.a: Strings are immutable, so each += builds a new string copying all previous characters. Over n steps this can be O(n^2). Better: collect characters in a list and use ''.join(list) at the end.

questions.q: What is the complexity of recursive code that calls f(n-1) twice?
questions.a: O(2^n). Each call spawns two calls, so the number of calls doubles per level for n levels.

questions.q: Optimise: for each number in a list count how many numbers are smaller than it.
questions.a: Brute force is O(n^2). Sort a copy, then use binary search (bisect_left) for each number: O(n log n). If values are small, a counting + prefix sum approach is O(n + k).

questions.q: What is the space complexity of recursion?
questions.a: O(depth of recursion) because each active call holds a frame. For a balanced tree that is O(log n); for a linked-list-shaped tree O(n).

questions.q: Can you improve O(n log n) sorting-based duplicate detection?
questions.a: Yes, use a set for O(n) average time at the price of O(n) space.

questions.q: A report is slow because it concatenates strings in a loop. Why?
questions.a: Each += copies the existing string, so n appends cost O(n^2) total. Collect parts in a list and ''.join them once.

questions.q: Why do nested loops multiply but sequential loops add?
questions.a: A nested inner loop runs fully for every iteration of the outer loop (n x m). Sequential loops run one after another (n + m).

questions.q: Why must you count recursion depth as space?
questions.a: Each active call holds a stack frame in memory. Depth d means d frames at once, which is O(d) extra space.

questions.q: Why is trading space for time common?
questions.a: Memory is cheap compared with time limits. A set or dictionary can remove an entire inner loop.

questions.q: Why not always choose the lowest time complexity?
questions.a: A lower complexity may use much more memory, be harder to write or be slower for small n. Choose the simplest solution that passes the limits.

questions.q: Why does slicing hide a cost?
questions.a: a[i:j] copies j - i elements, so a slice inside a loop can turn O(n) into O(n^2).

questions.q: Why is 'x in list' risky inside a loop?
questions.a: It scans the list: O(n) per check, so the loop becomes O(n^2). Use a set for O(1) average membership.

questions.q: What is the complexity of sorting inside a loop that runs n times on a list of size n?
questions.a: O(n^2 log n). Each sort costs O(n log n) and it runs n times.

questions.q: How do you analyse a function that calls itself with n/2 twice and does O(1) extra work?
questions.a: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1, which solves to O(n): the recursion tree has n leaves and about n total nodes.

questions.q: How do you reverse a list in Python? Give two ways.
questions.a:
```
nums.reverse()        # in place, O(1) extra space
rev = nums[::-1]      # new reversed list, O(n) extra space
```
You can also write the two-pointer swap loop yourself.

questions.q: Why is inserting at the front of a list slow?
questions.a: Every existing element has to move one position to the right to make room, so it takes O(n). If you need fast inserts at both ends, use collections.deque.

questions.q: How do you find the second largest element in one pass?
questions.a: Keep two variables first and second. For each x: if x > first then second = first and first = x; elif first > x > second then second = x. Return second (or -1 if it never changed). O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: How do you remove duplicates from a sorted list in place?
questions.a: Use a write pointer w starting at 1. For each element after the first, if it differs from nums[w-1], copy it to nums[w] and increase w. The first w items are the unique values.

questions.q: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
questions.a: A shallow copy (a[:] or list(a)) creates a new outer list but the inner objects are shared. For a list of lists, changing an inner list changes both copies. A deep copy (copy.deepcopy) copies everything recursively.

questions.q: Why is array indexing O(1)?
questions.a: Elements sit in contiguous memory in equal-sized slots, so the address of element i is base + i x size, computed in one step. In Python the slots hold pointers.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)
```
questions.a: [1, 2, 3, 4]. b = a copies the reference, not the list; both names point at the same object.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
grid = [[0] * 2] * 2
grid[0][0] = 5
print(grid)
```
questions.a: [[5, 0], [5, 0]]. Both rows are the same list object. Use [[0] * 2 for _ in range(2)].

questions.q: Reverse an array in place and explain complexity.
questions.a:
```
def reverse(a):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
        lo += 1
        hi -= 1
```
O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

questions.q: How would you remove all occurrences of a value in place in O(n)?
questions.a: Reader/writer pointers: copy non-matching items to the write index and return that index as the new length.

questions.q: Why do image libraries use arrays instead of linked lists?
questions.a: Pixel access by coordinates must be O(1) and processing scans memory sequentially, which is fast for contiguous data thanks to CPU caching.

questions.q: Why do list indexes start at 0?
questions.a: The index is the distance from the first element. The first element is 0 steps away, so its offset is 0. It also makes address arithmetic simple.

questions.q: Why is inserting in the middle slow?
questions.a: Items sit side by side, so everything after the insertion point must move one place to make room: O(n).

questions.q: Why not use a list as a queue?
questions.a: pop(0) shifts every remaining element: O(n). Use collections.deque for O(1) at both ends.

questions.q: Why does b = a not copy a list?
questions.a: Assignment copies the reference (the label), not the object. Both names point at the same list. Use a[:] or list(a) to copy.

questions.q: Why is append fast even though the list occasionally resizes?
questions.a: Python allocates extra spare room, so most appends just use a free slot. The rare resize cost is spread over many appends (amortised O(1)).

questions.q: Why use enumerate instead of range(len(nums))?
questions.a: enumerate gives index and value together, is clearer, and avoids indexing mistakes. Use range(len(...)) only when you really need to change items by index.

questions.q: What does a = [1, 2, 3]; print(a[1:], a[:-1], a[::-1]) print?
Write a function that returns True if a list is sorted in non-decreasing order.
How do you find duplicates in a list in O(n)?
questions.a: Count with a dictionary or Counter, then collect keys whose count is above 1. Or use a seen set and record an item when it is already in the set.

questions.q: How do you find the missing number from 0..n in O(n) time and O(1) space?
questions.a: expected = n * (n + 1) // 2 and the answer is expected - sum(nums). XOR of all indices and values also works.

questions.q: How would you rotate an array by k in place?
questions.a: Do k %= n, reverse the whole array, reverse the first k elements, reverse the remaining n - k elements. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: How do you find the element that appears once when all others appear twice?
questions.a: XOR all the numbers. Equal numbers cancel (x ^ x = 0) and 0 ^ y = y, so only the single number remains.

questions.q: What is the Boyer-Moore voting algorithm?
questions.a: It finds an element appearing more than n/2 times in O(1) space. Keep a candidate and a count. Same number: count + 1, different number: count - 1, when count is 0 pick a new candidate. The true majority cannot be fully cancelled out.

questions.q: Find the first non-repeating number in a list in O(n).
Do it with O(1) extra space when numbers are in the range 1..n.
questions.a: Use the array itself as a counter by marking visited values with sign changes or by storing counts at index value, if modifying the input is allowed.

questions.q: What does Counter('aab') - Counter('abb') produce?
questions.a: Counter({'a': 1}). Subtraction keeps only positive counts: a has 2 - 1 = 1; b has 1 - 2 < 0 and is dropped.

questions.q: Why does XOR find the single number?
questions.a: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, and XOR is order-independent, so every pair cancels and only the single number remains.

questions.q: How would you find duplicate user IDs in a file with 10 million lines that does not fit memory?
questions.a: Hash partition the IDs into many smaller files (same ID always lands in the same file) and check duplicates per file with a set, or use external sorting.

questions.q: Why use a dictionary to count instead of count() in a loop?
questions.a: list.count(x) scans the whole list, so calling it for every element is O(n^2). One dictionary pass is O(n).

questions.q: Why does XOR find the single number?
questions.a: XOR cancels equal numbers (x ^ x = 0) and does not care about order, so only the unpaired value survives.

questions.q: Why not just sort to find duplicates?
questions.a: Sorting works (equal items become neighbours) but costs O(n log n). A set or Counter is O(n).

questions.q: Why take k %= n before rotating?
questions.a: Rotating by n returns the original list, so only the remainder matters. It also prevents index errors for large k.

questions.q: Why is the sum formula safe in Python but risky elsewhere?
questions.a: Python integers do not overflow. In C/Java n(n+1)/2 can exceed 32-bit limits, so XOR is safer there.

questions.q: Why not use a list of size max(nums) as a counter for any data?
questions.a: If values are huge (10^9) the list needs gigabytes. Use a dictionary when the value range is large or unknown.

questions.q: Return the element that appears exactly once when all others appear three times.
questions.a: Count bits: for each bit position sum the bits across all numbers modulo 3; the remaining bits form the answer. O(32 n) time, O(1) space. A Counter is simpler (O(n) space).

questions.q: What does Counter([1, 1, 2]).most_common(1) return?
questions.a: [(1, 2)]: the most common element and its count.

questions.q: Explain Kadane's algorithm.
questions.a: Scan once with cur = best sum of a subarray that ends at the current element. cur = max(x, cur + x) (extend or restart), best = max(best, cur). Time O(n), space O(1). Start best at nums[0] so all-negative arrays work.

questions.q: How do prefix sums speed up range queries?
questions.a: Precompute prefix[i] once in O(n). Then sum(l..r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] in O(1) instead of looping each time.

questions.q: How do you count subarrays with sum exactly k, even with negative numbers?
questions.a: Keep a running prefix sum and a dictionary of prefix frequencies starting with {0: 1}. For each element add count[prefix - k] to the answer, then record the current prefix. O(n) time.

questions.q: Why does sliding window fail when the array has negative numbers?
questions.a: Window logic relies on 'adding an element increases the sum, removing decreases it'. With negatives that is not true, so you cannot decide whether to shrink or grow. Use prefix sums + hash map instead.

questions.q: What do you return if the array is all negative in the maximum subarray problem?
questions.a: The largest single element (the least negative). That is why best must start at nums[0], not 0.

questions.q: Return the start and end index of the maximum subarray.
What about a circular array (the subarray may wrap around)?
questions.a: Answer = max(Kadane max, total sum - Kadane min). If all numbers are negative the wrap case must be ignored (return the Kadane max).

questions.q: What does Kadane return for [-1, -2, -3] if best starts at 0?
questions.a: 0, which is wrong (an empty subarray) if the problem requires a non-empty one. Start best with the first element.

questions.q: Why do prefix sums fail for 'range maximum'?
questions.a: Subtraction undoes addition but nothing undoes max. Use a sparse table or segment tree for range max.

questions.q: How would you answer 'sales between any two dates' on a dashboard with a million rows?
questions.a: Pre-aggregate daily totals and store cumulative sums so any range is two lookups, or use database indexes/window functions.

questions.q: Why does the prefix array start with 0?
questions.a: So that sum(l..r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] also works when l = 0 without a special case.

questions.q: Why does Kadane restart when the running sum is negative?
questions.a: A negative running sum can only lower any future subarray total, so the best choice is to start fresh at the current element.

questions.q: Why not use sliding window for max subarray with negatives?
questions.a: Windows assume that shrinking changes the sum in a known direction. Negative numbers break that assumption.

questions.q: Why use prefix sums instead of recalculating each query?
questions.a: Q queries on n items cost O(Qn) recalculating but only O(n + Q) with prefix sums.

questions.q: Why initialise best with nums[0] and not 0?
questions.a: If all numbers are negative the true answer is negative. Starting at 0 would wrongly return 0 (an empty subarray).

questions.q: Why can't prefix sums answer range maximum queries?
questions.a: There is no inverse operation for max: knowing the max up to r and the max up to l-1 does not tell you the max of the middle part.

questions.q: Count subarrays with sum equal to k using prefix sums.
questions.a:
```
def count(nums, k):
    seen, pre, ans = {0: 1}, 0, 0
    for x in nums:
        pre += x
        ans += seen.get(pre - k, 0)
        seen[pre] = seen.get(pre, 0) + 1
    return ans
```

questions.q: How do you answer many range queries when values also change?
questions.a: Use a Fenwick tree or segment tree: O(log n) per update and query.

questions.q: Are strings mutable in Python? What does that mean for your code?
questions.a: No, they are immutable. You cannot write s[0] = 'x'. To change text, build a new string, or convert to a list (list(s)), edit it and join it back with ''.join(list).

questions.q: How do you check if a string is a palindrome ignoring case and punctuation?
questions.a: Use two pointers. Skip characters where not ch.isalnum(), compare lower-case versions, and move inward. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: What is the difference between split() and split(' ')?
questions.a: split() splits on any amount of whitespace and drops empty pieces. split(' ') splits on every single space, so 'a  b' (two spaces) gives ['a', '', 'b'].

questions.q: How do you count vowels in a string?
How would you reverse the words in a sentence?
questions.a:
```
' '.join(reversed(s.split()))
```
split() handles extra spaces, reversed() flips the list, join glues it back.

questions.q: What is the complexity of s[::-1]?
questions.a: O(n) time and O(n) space because it creates a new reversed string.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
s = 'hello'
print(s[1:4], s[-3:], s[::2])
```
questions.a: ell llo hlo. s[1:4] = indexes 1,2,3; s[-3:] = last three; s[::2] = every second character.

questions.q: Why is building a string with += in a loop discouraged?
questions.a: Strings are immutable, so each += may copy the whole string, giving O(n^2) total. Append to a list and join once.

questions.q: Check if a string is a palindrome ignoring case and non-alphanumerics, in O(1) extra space.
Find the longest palindromic substring.
questions.a: Expand around each centre (odd and even) and keep the longest: O(n^2) time, O(1) space. Manacher's algorithm achieves O(n) but is rarely required.

questions.q: Why do systems normalise text to lowercase before comparing?
questions.a: Users type 'Email' and 'email' expecting the same result. Normalising (case, whitespace, Unicode form) makes comparisons consistent.

questions.q: Why are Python strings immutable?
questions.a: Immutability lets Python share strings safely, cache their hashes and use them as dictionary keys, which makes common operations fast.

questions.q: Why not build strings with += in a loop?
questions.a: Each += can copy the whole string, making n appends O(n^2). Append to a list and ''.join() once.

questions.q: Why is slicing end-exclusive?
questions.a: It makes lengths simple (s[a:b] has b - a characters) and lets s[:k] + s[k:] rebuild s with no overlap.

questions.q: Why use two pointers for palindromes?
questions.a: It uses O(1) extra space and can stop at the first mismatch, instead of building a reversed copy.

questions.q: Why lower-case before comparing?
questions.a: 'A' and 'a' are different characters. Normalising case makes comparisons match what humans mean.

questions.q: Why not use == to test that two strings are the same object?
questions.a: == compares values; 'is' compares identity. Equal strings may or may not be the same object, so 'is' on text gives unreliable results.

questions.q: Count words in a sentence without using split().
What does 'abc'.find('d') return, and what does 'abc'.index('d') do?
questions.a: find returns -1; index raises ValueError.

questions.q: How do you check if two strings are anagrams?
questions.a: Check lengths first. Then compare Counter(s) == Counter(t) (O(n)) or sorted(s) == sorted(t) (O(n log n)).

questions.q: How do you find the first non-repeating character?
questions.a: Count all characters with a Counter in one pass, then scan the string again from the left and return the index of the first character with count 1. If none, return -1.

questions.q: How do you group anagrams together?
questions.a: Use a dictionary with the sorted letters of each word as the key and a list of words as the value. Return list(d.values()).

questions.q: Why use a 26-element list instead of a dictionary for lowercase letters?
questions.a: It uses fixed small memory and is a little faster since indexing a list is quicker than hashing. Both are O(n) overall.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of checking anagrams with sorting vs counting?
questions.a: Sorting: O(n log n). Counting: O(n) time and O(k) space where k is the alphabet size.

questions.q: Group anagrams using a count signature instead of sorting.
Is 'Listen' an anagram of 'Silent' in a case-sensitive check?
questions.a: No: 'L' differs from 'l'. Normalise with .lower() when the problem says case does not matter.

questions.q: How do you check if one string contains a permutation of another?
questions.a: Fixed sliding window of length len(s1) over s2 with counts updated incrementally.

questions.q: What is a canonical form and why is it useful?
questions.a: A single standard representation for all equivalent items (sorted letters for anagrams). It lets you test equality by one comparison or use it as a hash key.

questions.q: How might a word-game helper find all words from a rack of tiles?
questions.a: Precompute each dictionary word's letter-count signature; a word fits if its counts are all <= the rack's counts.

questions.q: Why check lengths first for anagrams?
questions.a: Different lengths can never be anagrams, so you can answer instantly without counting.

questions.q: Why does a 26-slot list beat a dictionary here?
questions.a: It needs no hashing and has a fixed small size, so it is faster, but it only works for known small alphabets.

questions.q: Why count first and scan second for the first unique character?
questions.a: You need the global counts before you can decide, but you need the original order to find the first. Two passes handle both.

questions.q: Why not compare sorted strings for huge inputs?
questions.a: Sorting costs O(n log n); counting is O(n).

questions.q: Why use Counter subtraction for ransom note?
questions.a: It removes the magazine's letters from the note's letters; an empty result means nothing is missing.

questions.q: Why can't a list be used as a dictionary key for a letter-count signature?
questions.a: Lists are mutable and unhashable. Convert it to a tuple.

questions.q: Find all start indices of anagrams of p in s.
questions.a: Slide a window of len(p) over s keeping letter counts; record the start when the window counts equal p's counts. O(n).

questions.q: Why do spell-check suggestions use letter frequencies?
questions.a: Words made of similar letters are likely typos of each other, and frequency vectors are cheap to compare.

questions.q: What is the naive pattern-matching time complexity and when is it bad?
questions.a: O(n x m). It is bad on inputs with many partial matches, like text 'aaaa...a' and pattern 'aaa...ab'.

questions.q: What is the idea behind KMP?
questions.a: Precompute the LPS table: for each prefix of the pattern, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. After a mismatch you use it to jump the pattern pointer back to the right place without moving the text pointer back. O(n + m) total.

questions.q: What is a hash collision in Rabin-Karp and how do you handle it?
questions.a: Two different strings can have the same hash number. When hashes match, compare the real characters to confirm.

questions.q: How can you check if one string is a rotation of another?
questions.a: Same length and s2 in s1 + s1. For example 'erbottlewat' is inside 'waterbottlewaterbottle'.

questions.q: What does the LPS array of 'abab' look like?
questions.a: [0, 0, 1, 2]. At index 3 the prefix 'ab' equals the suffix 'ab', so the value is 2.

questions.q: Return the index of the first occurrence of pattern in text, or -1, without using find.
How would you find the longest prefix that is also a suffix?
questions.a: Build the LPS table of the string; the last value lps[-1] is the answer.

questions.q: What is a hash collision and why does Rabin-Karp still work?
questions.a: Two different strings share a hash. Rabin-Karp verifies equal-hash candidates with a direct comparison, so correctness is kept; collisions only cost time.

questions.q: What does 'aaaa'.count('aa') return?
questions.a: 2. count() counts non-overlapping occurrences; overlapping matches would be 3.

questions.q: How can an app search millions of documents quickly for a word?
questions.a: Build an inverted index (word -> list of documents) so searches are lookups, not scans. Scanning algorithms handle the within-document step.

questions.q: Why not always use KMP?
questions.a: Python's built-in find is highly tuned and simpler. KMP matters when asked to implement it, or when you need guaranteed linear time or the LPS table.

questions.q: Why verify after a hash match in Rabin-Karp?
questions.a: Different strings can have the same hash (a collision). Verification keeps the answer correct.

questions.q: Why does KMP never move the text pointer backwards?
questions.a: The LPS table already tells how much of the pattern is still matched, so no text needs to be re-read.

questions.q: Why use a large prime modulus in rolling hashes?
questions.a: Large primes spread hash values evenly and make collisions rare.

questions.q: Why is naive search usually fine in practice?
questions.a: Mismatches typically occur early, so the average cost is near O(n). Only adversarial inputs make it quadratic.

questions.q: Why is str.count not enough for overlapping matches?
questions.a: count() skips past each match, so 'aaaa'.count('aa') is 2, not 3. Use find in a loop with start = idx + 1.

questions.q: Check whether a string is made by repeating a smaller substring.
questions.a:
```
def repeated(s):
    return s in (s + s)[1:-1]
```

questions.q: What is a proper prefix?
questions.a: A prefix that is not the whole string. The LPS table only considers proper prefixes.

questions.q: Why is binary search O(log n)?
questions.a: Each comparison halves the search window. After k steps the window has n / 2^k items; it becomes 1 when k = log2(n).

questions.q: Can you use binary search on an unsorted array?
questions.a: No. The decision 'go left or right' only works because the data is ordered. You would first have to sort it (O(n log n)), which only pays off for many searches.

questions.q: What is the difference between lo <= hi and lo < hi loops?
questions.a: With lo <= hi and both ends inclusive you check every position including the last one; you use mid + 1 / mid - 1. With lo < hi and hi = len(nums) (half-open) you use hi = mid to keep a candidate. Pick one style and stick with it.

questions.q: Write iterative binary search.
When is linear search better than binary search?
questions.a: For tiny lists, for unsorted data you only search once, or when the list is a linked list (no random access).

questions.q: What does bisect_left([1, 2, 2, 3], 2) return?
questions.a: 1: the first index where 2 could be inserted (before the existing 2s). bisect_right returns 3.

questions.q: Find the index of the first element >= x in a sorted list.
Why must the array be sorted?
questions.a: The comparison with the middle element must tell you which half can contain the target; without order the discarded half might contain it.

questions.q: How many comparisons for n = 10^9?
questions.a: About 30, since log2(10^9) is roughly 30.

questions.q: How does git bisect find a faulty commit?
questions.a: It marks one good and one bad commit, tests the middle commit, and halves the range each time, finding the first bad commit in O(log n) tests.

questions.q: Describe a time you used a divide-and-narrow approach to debug.
questions.a: Strong answers describe cutting the search space in half repeatedly: comment out half the code, check logs at the midpoint of a pipeline, or bisect commits until the faulty change is isolated.

questions.q: Why must the list be sorted for binary search?
questions.a: The comparison with the middle element tells you which half to discard only if the data is ordered.

questions.q: Why not always sort and binary search?
questions.a: Sorting costs O(n log n). For a single search a linear scan (O(n)) is cheaper.

questions.q: Why is lo <= hi the loop condition?
questions.a: When lo equals hi there is still one candidate left to check. Using < would skip it.

questions.q: Why mid + 1 and mid - 1 instead of mid?
questions.a: mid has already been checked. Excluding it guarantees the window shrinks and the loop ends.

questions.q: Why can (lo + hi) // 2 overflow in other languages?
questions.a: lo + hi may exceed the integer limit. lo + (hi - lo) // 2 is safe. Python has no overflow.

questions.q: Why not use binary search on a linked list?
questions.a: Reaching the middle of a linked list takes O(n), so the O(log n) benefit disappears.

questions.q: Search for a target in a sorted list using recursion.
How many steps does binary search take on 8 items in the worst case?
questions.a: 4 comparisons at most (3 halvings plus the final check), about log2(8) + 1.

questions.q: How do you find the first and last position of a target in a sorted array?
questions.a: Run binary search twice. When nums[mid] == target save mid and continue left (hi = mid - 1) for the first position, or right (lo = mid + 1) for the last. O(log n) each.

questions.q: How do you search in a rotated sorted array?
questions.a: At each step one half is sorted. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid] the left half is sorted; check if the target is in [nums[lo], nums[mid]) and go there, else go right. The other case is symmetric. O(log n).

questions.q: How do you find the insertion position of a value?
questions.a: It is the lower bound: the first index whose value is >= target. In Python: bisect.bisect_left(nums, target).

questions.q: How do you count how many times x appears in a sorted array?
questions.a: bisect_right(a, x) - bisect_left(a, x), or last - first + 1 using two binary searches. O(log n).

questions.q: What if the rotated array contains duplicates?
questions.a: Sometimes nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] and you cannot tell which half is sorted. You then shrink lo and hi by one. Worst case becomes O(n).

questions.q: Count occurrences of x in a sorted list in O(log n).
For [1, 3, 5, 7], what does bisect_left give for 4 and for 8?
questions.a: 2 and 4. 4 would be inserted before 5 (index 2); 8 goes at the end (index 4 = len).

questions.q: Find the floor (largest value <= x) in a sorted list.
questions.a: i = bisect_right(a, x) - 1; return a[i] if i >= 0 else None.

questions.q: Why does the rotated search always find one sorted half?
questions.a: Rotation splits the sorted list into two sorted runs. Any cut at mid leaves at least one side fully inside one run.

questions.q: Where would you use lower_bound in a real system?
questions.a: Finding the first log entry after a timestamp, the first free time slot, the insertion index for a sorted playlist or pagination cursors.

questions.q: Why keep searching after finding the target for first/last occurrence?
questions.a: The target may appear many times. Continuing left finds the first copy; continuing right finds the last.

questions.q: Why does the rotated array search work?
questions.a: After cutting at mid one side is always sorted, so you can check whether the target lies inside that sorted range.

questions.q: Why use hi = len(a) for lower_bound?
questions.a: The answer can be len(a) (insert at the end), so the search range must include that position.

questions.q: Why not scan linearly from the match to find the first occurrence?
questions.a: With many duplicates that costs O(n). A second binary search keeps O(log n).

questions.q: Why compare with a[hi] when finding the rotated minimum?
questions.a: a[hi] tells which side of mid contains the drop. If a[mid] > a[hi] the minimum is to the right.

questions.q: Why does duplicate data hurt the rotated search?
questions.a: When a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi] you cannot tell which half is sorted, so you must shrink by one and the worst case becomes O(n).

questions.q: Find the ceiling (smallest value >= x) in a sorted list.
questions.a: i = bisect_left(a, x); return a[i] if i < len(a) else None.

questions.q: bisect_right([1, 2, 2, 3], 2) - bisect_left([1, 2, 2, 3], 2) equals?
questions.a: 2, the number of 2s.

questions.q: What is 'binary search on the answer'?
questions.a: Instead of searching in an array, you search the range of possible answers. You need a yes/no function that switches from No to Yes exactly once as the candidate grows. Then you halve the range each step.

questions.q: Explain how to find the minimum capacity to ship packages in D days.
questions.a: Capacity is between max(weights) and sum(weights). For a capacity c, simulate loading days greedily and count days. If days <= D then c works (try smaller), else try bigger. O(n log(sum)).

questions.q: How do you compute the integer square root without sqrt?
questions.a: Binary search x in [0, n]: if mid * mid <= n it could be the answer (lo = mid + 1 and remember mid), else hi = mid - 1.

questions.q: Why do you need the monotonic property?
questions.a: Because the decision at mid must tell you which half to discard. If the yes/no answers were mixed randomly you could not safely throw half away.

questions.q: How do you avoid an infinite loop when maximising?
questions.a: Use mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2 with lo = mid on success so the range always shrinks.

questions.q: Find the smallest divisor such that the sum of ceil(a_i / d) is <= threshold.
What does 'monotonic predicate' mean?
questions.a: A yes/no function whose answers switch at most once as the input increases (all No then all Yes, or the reverse).

questions.q: How do you handle 'maximise the minimum distance' (placing routers)?
questions.a: Binary search the distance d; check greedily whether you can place k routers at least d apart. On success try a larger d (lo = mid), else a smaller one.

questions.q: Why can lo = mid cause an infinite loop?
questions.a: With mid = (lo + hi) // 2 and lo = mid, when hi = lo + 1 then mid = lo and nothing changes. Use mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2 for that style.

questions.q: How does an autoscaler pick the smallest number of servers that handles peak traffic?
questions.a: It can binary search the server count, simulating load for each candidate; fewer servers means more overload, which is monotonic.

questions.q: Why can you binary search something that is not an array?
questions.a: You search the range of possible answers using a yes/no check that is monotonic.

questions.q: Why must the check be monotonic?
questions.a: Otherwise the result at mid does not tell you which half to discard.

questions.q: Why not try every possible answer?
questions.a: The range can be 10^9 wide. Binary search needs only about 30 checks.

questions.q: Why is the lower bound often max(weights)?
questions.a: Capacity below the heaviest item can never work.

questions.q: Why use ceil division in the feasibility check?
questions.a: A pile of 7 at speed 3 takes 3 hours (not 2.33) because partial hours count as full.

questions.q: Why does the answer-search use hi = mid on success when minimising?
questions.a: mid might itself be the smallest working value, so it must stay in the range.

questions.q: Find the integer cube root of n by binary search.
How could you use this idea to size a server pool?
questions.a: Binary search the number of servers; simulate the load for each candidate and pick the smallest count that meets the target latency.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of bubble sort? Can it be improved?
questions.a: O(n^2) in the worst and average case. With a flag that stops when a pass has no swaps, the best case (already sorted) becomes O(n).

questions.q: What does a stable sort mean?
questions.a: Equal elements keep their original relative order. This matters when you sort records by one field and want a previous order kept for ties.

questions.q: Which simple sort makes the fewest swaps?
questions.a: Selection sort makes at most n - 1 swaps, which is useful when writing to memory is expensive.

questions.q: Which simple sort is best for nearly sorted data?
questions.a: Insertion sort, because each element only moves a short distance. It runs in about O(n).

questions.q: Write insertion sort.
How many swaps does bubble sort make on [4, 3, 2, 1]?
questions.a: 6 swaps, equal to the number of inversions n(n-1)/2 = 6 for a reversed list.

questions.q: Which O(n^2) sort is best for almost sorted data and why?
questions.a: Insertion sort: it shifts each element only past larger neighbours, so work is proportional to the number of inversions, close to O(n).

questions.q: Implement selection sort.
How do you make a stable version of selection sort?
questions.a: Instead of swapping, shift the elements between i and m one step right and place the minimum at i (insertion-like), keeping equal elements in order.

questions.q: Why is stability important when sorting rows of a table by multiple columns?
questions.a: You can sort by the secondary key first and the primary key second; a stable sort preserves the earlier order within equal primary keys.

questions.q: Why learn bubble sort when nobody uses it?
questions.a: It teaches comparisons, swaps, invariants and counting operations. These ideas explain every other sort.

questions.q: Why is insertion sort fast on nearly sorted data?
questions.a: Each element moves only a short distance, so total shifts equal the small number of inversions.

questions.q: Why is selection sort not stable?
questions.a: Its long-distance swap can jump an element over an equal one, changing their original order.

questions.q: Why not use O(n^2) sorts for big inputs?
questions.a: n = 10^5 means 10^10 steps. Use sorted() or merge/quick sort.

questions.q: Why add a swapped flag to bubble sort?
questions.a: If a pass makes no swap, the list is sorted, so you can stop early.

questions.q: Why does stability matter?
questions.a: When you sort by a second key, a stable sort keeps the order produced by the first sort for equal items.

questions.q: Count the number of swaps selection sort makes on [3, 1, 2].
questions.a: 2 swaps: place 1 at the front, then 2 at the middle. At most n - 1 swaps.

questions.q: How many comparisons does bubble sort (without early exit) make on 5 items?
Compare merge sort and quick sort.
questions.a: Merge sort: always O(n log n), stable, needs O(n) extra space. Quick sort: average O(n log n), worst O(n^2), in place (O(log n) stack), not stable. Quick sort is usually faster in practice due to cache friendliness.

questions.q: What is the worst case of quick sort and how do you avoid it?
questions.a: O(n^2) when partitions are very unbalanced, e.g. an already sorted array with the last element as pivot. Avoid it with a random pivot or median-of-three.

questions.q: What is the recurrence of merge sort?
questions.a: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), which solves to O(n log n).

questions.q: How can merge sort count inversions?
questions.a: While merging, when an element from the right half is placed before elements still left in the left half, add len(left) - i to the count. Total O(n log n).

questions.q: Why is merge sort good for linked lists?
questions.a: Merging needs only pointer changes and no random access, so it is O(n log n) with O(1) extra space on lists.

questions.q: Write the merge step.
Why is merge sort stable and quick sort not?
questions.a: Merge sort takes from the left half when values are equal, preserving order. Quick sort's partition swaps elements across the pivot and may reorder equal values.

questions.q: Find the k-th smallest element faster than sorting (average O(n)).
questions.a: Quickselect: partition around a pivot; if the pivot index equals k - 1 you are done, else recurse into one side. Average O(n), worst O(n^2). Python alternative: heapq.nsmallest(k, a)[-1].

questions.q: What happens to quick sort on an already sorted array with the last element as pivot?
questions.a: Each partition splits into sizes n-1 and 0, so depth is n and total time O(n^2); recursion may also hit Python's limit.

questions.q: How would you sort a 50 GB file with 2 GB of RAM?
questions.a: External merge sort: sort 2 GB chunks in memory, write them out, then k-way merge the sorted chunks with a heap while reading sequentially.

questions.q: Why does Python's sort guarantee stability?
questions.a: Users often sort by multiple keys in passes; guaranteed stability makes that pattern correct and predictable.

questions.q: Why does merge sort always take O(n log n)?
questions.a: It halves the list log n times and each level merges n items, regardless of the order of the input.

questions.q: Why can quick sort be O(n^2)?
questions.a: If the pivot is always the smallest or largest, one side is empty and the depth becomes n.

questions.q: Why use a random pivot?
questions.a: No fixed input can force the worst case, so bad splits become extremely unlikely.

questions.q: Why does merge sort need extra memory?
questions.a: Merging two halves needs a place to write the combined result.

questions.q: Why is quick sort usually faster in practice?
questions.a: It sorts in place and scans memory sequentially, which uses the CPU cache well.

questions.q: Why is merge sort preferred for linked lists?
questions.a: Merging uses only pointer changes and sequential access, giving O(n log n) with O(1) extra space; quick sort needs random access.

questions.q: Merge two sorted lists into one sorted list.
How do you sort a list too big for memory?
questions.a: Sort chunks that fit in memory, write them to disk, then k-way merge them with a heap (external merge sort).

questions.q: When is counting sort a good choice?
questions.a: When the range of values k is small compared to n, such as marks 0-100 or lowercase letters. Time O(n + k), space O(k).

questions.q: What sorting algorithm does Python use?
questions.a: Timsort: a stable hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort, O(n log n) worst case and fast on partially sorted data.

questions.q: Is heap sort stable? Is it in place?
questions.a: In place: yes. Stable: no.

questions.q: How do you sort a list of tuples by the second item descending and the first ascending?
questions.a:
```
sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))
```

questions.q: What is the lower bound of comparison-based sorting?
questions.a: Omega(n log n). Any algorithm that only compares items needs at least about n log n comparisons. Counting sort avoids this by not comparing.

questions.q: Can you sort faster than O(n log n)?
questions.a: Yes, when you are not limited to comparisons and know something about the data: counting sort O(n + k), radix sort O(d(n + k)), bucket sort O(n) on uniform data. For general comparison-based sorting n log n is the lower bound.

questions.q: Sort an array containing only 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass.
questions.a: Dutch national flag: lo, mid, hi pointers; swap 0s to the front and 2s to the back, skip 1s. O(n), O(1) space.

questions.q: What does sorted([3, -1, -2], key=abs) return?
questions.a: [-1, -2, 3]. The key abs gives 3, 1, 2; sorted by that: -1 (1), -2 (2), 3 (3).

questions.q: Sort the characters of a string by decreasing frequency.
questions.a: Counter + sorted by key (-count, char), then repeat each char count times and join.

questions.q: How would you rank 10 million exam scores in the range 0-100?
questions.a: Counting sort (a 101-slot tally) in a single pass O(n), far faster than comparison sorting.

questions.q: Why can counting sort beat n log n?
questions.a: It does not compare items; it uses the values as indexes. The n log n bound applies only to comparison sorts.

questions.q: Why not use counting sort for any list?
questions.a: If the value range is huge (like 10^9), the count array needs too much memory.

questions.q: Why use heap sort?
questions.a: It guarantees O(n log n) and sorts in place with O(1) extra memory.

questions.q: Why is Timsort fast on real data?
questions.a: Real data often has ordered runs. Timsort detects and merges them, doing less work than n log n.

questions.q: Why sort with key= instead of cmp?
questions.a: A key is computed once per element and is faster and simpler than comparing pairs with a function.

questions.q: Why sort by negative frequency to get descending order?
questions.a: sorted sorts ascending. Negating the number reverses the order for that field without reversing the others.

questions.q: Sort a list of 0s and 1s in O(n) without sort().
questions.a: Count zeros and ones then rebuild: [0] * zeros + [1] * ones. Or two pointers swapping.

questions.q: What does sorted(['b', 'A', 'a', 'B']) return?
questions.a: ['A', 'B', 'a', 'b']. Uppercase codes come before lowercase. Use key=str.lower for case-insensitive order.

questions.q: How does a hash table work?
questions.a: A hash function converts a key into an integer. The integer picks a bucket where the key-value pair is stored. Lookup recomputes the hash and goes straight to the bucket, so it is O(1) on average.

questions.q: What is a hash collision and how is it handled?
questions.a: Two keys map to the same bucket. Handled by chaining (store several items in one bucket) or open addressing (probe for the next free slot).

questions.q: Why can't a list be a dictionary key?
questions.a: Lists are mutable, so their hash would change when they change. Use a tuple instead.

questions.q: What is the worst-case time of a dict lookup?
questions.a: O(n) if all keys collide into one bucket, but with a good hash function and resizing this practically never happens; average is O(1).

questions.q: What is the difference between a set and a dict?
questions.a: A set stores only unique keys. A dict stores key-value pairs. Both use hashing and have O(1) average lookup.

questions.q: How do you count word frequencies?
questions.a:
```
from collections import Counter
freq = Counter(text.split())
```

questions.q: Explain how a hash table handles collisions.
questions.a: Chaining stores all colliding entries in a list at that slot. Open addressing probes other slots (linear, quadratic or double hashing) until it finds an empty one. Both rely on resizing so load stays low.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```
d = {}
d[[1, 2]] = 'x'
```
questions.a: TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'. Lists are mutable; use a tuple (1, 2) as the key.

questions.q: What is the result of {1: 'a', True: 'b'}?
questions.a: {1: 'b'}. True == 1 and hash(True) == hash(1), so they are the same key; the value is overwritten.

questions.q: Implement a simple hash map with chaining.
What happens when the table gets too full and how do you fix it?
questions.a: Chains grow and operations slow down. Resize to a larger table and rehash all keys; the cost is O(n) but amortised over many inserts.

questions.q: How does a web cache use a hash table?
questions.a: The URL is the key and the stored response the value; a request is a single O(1) lookup, and an eviction policy (like LRU) decides what to drop when memory is full.

questions.q: Why is dictionary lookup O(1) on average?
questions.a: A hash function turns the key into a slot number, so Python jumps straight to it instead of scanning.

questions.q: Why can't lists be dictionary keys?
questions.a: Lists can change, so their hash would change. Keys must be unchangeable (hashable).

questions.q: Why does resizing keep dictionaries fast?
questions.a: When the table gets crowded Python rebuilds it bigger, so each slot holds about one item and collisions stay rare.

questions.q: Why use a set instead of a list for membership tests?
questions.a: 'x in set' is O(1) on average; 'x in list' is O(n).

questions.q: Why not use a dictionary when you need sorted order?
questions.a: Hash tables do not keep keys in sorted order. Use a sorted list or tree for ordered queries.

questions.q: Why does Python randomise string hashes?
questions.a: To prevent attackers from crafting many colliding keys that would slow a server down (a hash-flooding attack).

questions.q: Find the first non-repeating word in a list of words.
questions.a: Count with Counter, then scan the original list and return the first word with count 1.

questions.q: What does len({1, 1.0, True}) print?
questions.a: 1. 1, 1.0 and True are equal and hash alike, so the set keeps one.

questions.q: Solve Two Sum in O(n).
What if the array is sorted and you must use O(1) extra space?
questions.a: Use two pointers at both ends: if the sum is too small move the left pointer right, too big move the right pointer left.

questions.q: How do you handle duplicates like [3, 3] target 6?
questions.a: Check the dictionary before inserting the current element. The first 3 is stored, and when the second 3 comes, 6 - 3 = 3 is found.

questions.q: How would you count the number of pairs with sum k?
questions.a: Keep a counter dictionary of previous values. For each x add counter[k - x] to the answer, then increase counter[x].

questions.q: What is the trade-off between the hash map and the two-pointer solution?
questions.a: Hash map: O(n) time and O(n) space, works on unsorted data. Two pointers: O(n) time (after O(n log n) sort) and O(1) space but needs sorted data and loses original indices.

questions.q: Count pairs (i < j) with a[i] + a[j] == k.
questions.a:
```
def count_pairs(a, k):
    seen, total = {}, 0
    for x in a:
        total += seen.get(k - x, 0)
        seen[x] = seen.get(x, 0) + 1
    return total
```

questions.q: Find all unique pairs, not just one.
questions.a: Use a set of seen values and a set of result pairs stored as (min, max); or sort + two pointers skipping duplicates.

questions.q: The numbers arrive as a stream and you must answer 'is there a pair?' after each arrival.
questions.a: Maintain the set of seen numbers; for each new x check k - x in the set before adding x. O(1) per element.

questions.q: Why does Two Sum fail on [3] with target 6 if you insert before checking?
questions.a: It would find 3 for 6 - 3 and pair the element with itself. Check first, then insert.

questions.q: Why is Two Sum O(n) even though a dict lookup could be O(n) worst case?
questions.a: Hash lookups are O(1) on average because hashing spreads keys evenly; worst case is theoretical and extremely unlikely with Python's dict.

questions.q: Why check the dictionary before inserting?
questions.a: So an element is never paired with itself; the partner must be an earlier element.

questions.q: Why does the dictionary store value to index?
questions.a: The answer needs indices, and the lookup key is the value we are searching for.

questions.q: Why not sort and use two pointers when indices are needed?
questions.a: Sorting destroys the original positions unless you store them separately.

questions.q: Why is the hash map solution O(n) space?
questions.a: In the worst case it stores every element before finding a pair.

questions.q: Why does [3, 3] with target 6 still work?
questions.a: When the second 3 arrives, the first 3 is already stored, and 6 - 3 = 3 is found.

questions.q: Why not use a hash map when memory is extremely limited?
questions.a: It needs O(n) extra space. With sorted data two pointers use O(1); otherwise sort first if indices are not needed.

questions.q: Two Sum on a sorted array returning 1-indexed positions.
questions.a: Use two pointers lo and hi; return [lo + 1, hi + 1] when the sum matches.

questions.q: Three Sum with a hash set instead of two pointers?
questions.a: Fix one number and run two-sum with a set on the rest: O(n^2), but duplicate handling is trickier than with sorting.

questions.q: How do you group anagrams?
questions.a: Use a dictionary: key = ''.join(sorted(word)), value = list of words. Return the dictionary values. Time O(n k log k).

questions.q: How do you find the longest consecutive sequence in O(n)?
questions.a: Put numbers in a set. For each x with x - 1 not in the set, count how far x, x+1, x+2... continue. Track the maximum length.

questions.q: Why is the longest-consecutive algorithm O(n) even though it has nested loops?
questions.a: The inner while loop only runs for the first number of each streak, and each number is visited at most once across all streaks.

questions.q: How do you check if two words follow the same letter pattern (isomorphic)?
questions.a: Keep two dictionaries mapping letters in both directions and check they stay consistent.

questions.q: How can you find common elements of two arrays?
questions.a: set(a) & set(b). Time O(n + m).

questions.q: Find all numbers that appear in all of three lists.
Group strings that are shifts of each other ('abc', 'bcd', 'xyz').
questions.a: Use the differences between consecutive characters (mod 26) as the key.

questions.q: What does set('hello') print and does the order matter?
questions.a: A set of unique letters such as {'h', 'e', 'l', 'o'}; order is not guaranteed.

questions.q: Why is the while loop inside the for loop in longest consecutive sequence not O(n^2)?
questions.a: It only runs for numbers that start a streak, and each number belongs to exactly one streak, so total inner iterations are at most n.

questions.q: How can you find duplicate files quickly?
questions.a: Group by file size, then by a hash of the contents (e.g. SHA-256), and compare bytes only for matching hashes.

questions.q: Why use sorted letters as the key for anagrams?
questions.a: All anagrams produce the same sorted string, so it is a canonical label for the group.

questions.q: Why only start counting at numbers whose predecessor is missing?
questions.a: Starting everywhere would recount each streak many times; starting only at streak beginnings counts each number about once.

questions.q: Why use a set for the longest consecutive sequence?
questions.a: It makes 'is x + 1 present?' an O(1) check.

questions.q: Why is defaultdict(list) handy?
questions.a: It creates an empty list for a missing key automatically, so groups can be appended to directly.

questions.q: Why sort the output when grouping?
questions.a: Dictionaries and sets may give arbitrary order; judges often expect a fixed order.

questions.q: Why not group anagrams by comparing every pair of words?
questions.a: That is O(n^2 k). A canonical key puts each word in its group in one step.

questions.q: Find the intersection of two arrays keeping duplicates (multiset).
questions.a: Use Counter(a) & Counter(b) and expand with .elements().

questions.q: How is 'group by canonical key' used in data cleaning?
questions.a: Normalising emails or names (lower-case, trimmed) and grouping by the normalised value finds duplicate customer records.

questions.q: When can you use the two pointer technique?
questions.a: When the data is sorted or has structure that tells you which pointer to move: pair sums in sorted arrays, palindromes, merging sorted lists, removing items in place, partitioning.

questions.q: Explain pair sum in a sorted array with two pointers.
questions.a: Put lo at the start and hi at the end. If nums[lo] + nums[hi] equals the target you are done; if it is smaller move lo right; if bigger move hi left. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: Solve 3Sum.
questions.a: Sort, then for each i skip duplicates and use two pointers lo = i + 1, hi = n - 1 to find pairs summing to -nums[i]. Skip duplicates after a hit. O(n^2).

questions.q: How does Container With Most Water work?
questions.a: Start with the widest container. Area = width x min(height). Move the pointer at the shorter line inward, because moving the taller one can never improve the area.

questions.q: What is the difference between two pointers and sliding window?
questions.a: Two pointers is the general idea of two moving indices. Sliding window is a special case where the two pointers define a contiguous range (a window) whose contents you keep track of.

questions.q: Check whether a sorted array has a pair with difference exactly d (d >= 0).
Why does the container-with-most-water pointer move the shorter side?
questions.a: The area is limited by the shorter line. Moving the taller line can only shrink the width without improving the height limit, so the shorter side is the only move that might increase the area.

questions.q: How do you solve 4Sum?
questions.a: Sort, fix two numbers with two loops and use two pointers for the rest: O(n^3). Skip duplicates at every level.

questions.q: Why should 3Sum skip duplicates after finding a triplet?
questions.a: Otherwise the same triplet values would be reported multiple times.

questions.q: Where is a two-pointer merge used in databases?
questions.a: Sort-merge joins walk two sorted inputs together to find matching keys in one pass.

questions.q: Why can you discard an element when the pair sum is too small?
questions.a: In a sorted list the left value is the smallest, so even paired with the largest it is too small; it can never be part of an answer.

questions.q: Why does two pointers need a sorted array?
questions.a: Sortedness tells you which pointer to move to increase or decrease the sum.

questions.q: Why not use a nested loop?
questions.a: It checks pairs that were already ruled out, costing O(n^2).

questions.q: Why skip duplicates in 3Sum?
questions.a: Otherwise the same triplet is reported more than once.

questions.q: Why does the reader/writer pointer never overwrite unread data?
questions.a: The writer index is always less than or equal to the reader index.

questions.q: Why can't two pointers solve pair sum on an unsorted array directly?
questions.a: Without order you cannot tell which pointer to move. Sort first (O(n log n)) or use a hash map.

questions.q: Merge two sorted arrays in place when the first has extra space at the end.
questions.a: Fill from the back using three pointers (last of each array and the write position) so no unread element is overwritten.

questions.q: For [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and target 9, which pair do two pointers find?
questions.a: (4, 5) at indices 3 and 4: starting at 1 + 5 = 6 (too small) the left pointer moves until 4 + 5.

questions.q: What is the sliding window technique?
questions.a: Maintain a window (range) over the data and move it step by step, updating the result incrementally instead of recomputing from scratch.

questions.q: Maximum sum of k consecutive elements - complexity?
questions.a: O(n) time and O(1) space using the sliding window. Brute force would be O(n k).

questions.q: How do you check if s2 contains a permutation of s1?
questions.a: Slide a window of size len(s1) over s2 and compare letter counts with s1 (Counter equality). Update counts by adding the entering letter and removing the leaving one.

questions.q: How do you find the maximum in every window of size k?
questions.a: Use a monotonic deque of indices whose values decrease. The front is the maximum; pop from the back while the back is smaller than the new element; pop from the front when it leaves the window. O(n).

questions.q: What edge cases should you test for fixed windows?
questions.a: k = 1, k = n, k > n, negative numbers, and an empty list.

questions.q: Find the maximum average of any k consecutive numbers.
questions.a:
```
def max_avg(a, k):
    w = sum(a[:k])
    best = w
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        w += a[i] - a[i - k]
        best = max(best, w)
    return best / k
```

questions.q: What is the answer if k > len(a)?
questions.a: Undefined for the problem; handle it explicitly (return -1 or raise) before the loop. This is a common hidden test.

questions.q: How do you find the maximum in every window of size k?
questions.a: Monotonic deque of indices with decreasing values; O(n).

questions.q: Why does the sliding window avoid recomputing?
questions.a: Consecutive windows share k - 1 elements, so only the entering and leaving elements change the result.

questions.q: How does an API rate limiter implement 'at most 100 requests per minute'?
questions.a: A sliding window of timestamps (deque): drop timestamps older than 60 seconds and reject if the remaining count is 100.

questions.q: Why is the sliding window faster than re-summing?
questions.a: Consecutive windows share k - 1 elements, so only one number enters and one leaves.

questions.q: Why build the first window separately?
questions.a: The update rule subtracts nums[i - k], which exists only after k elements have been added.

questions.q: Why check k > n first?
questions.a: No window of size k exists, and slicing or indexing would give a wrong or empty result.

questions.q: Why does a plain sum update not work for window maximum?
questions.a: You cannot 'subtract' a maximum. A monotonic deque is used instead.

questions.q: Why is the answer O(1) space?
questions.a: Only the running window value and the best value are stored.

questions.q: Why not use prefix sums for fixed windows?
questions.a: You can: window sum = prefix[i + k] - prefix[i]. It costs O(n) memory but supports any range; the window uses O(1) memory.

questions.q: Count the number of windows of size k with sum at least t.
questions.a: Slide the window and increment a counter whenever the running sum >= t.

questions.q: For nums = [1, 2, 3] and k = 3, how many windows exist?
questions.a: Exactly one: n - k + 1 = 1.

questions.q: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
Smallest subarray with sum at least target (all positive numbers)?
questions.a: Expand right adding to a sum; while sum >= target record the length and subtract nums[left], left += 1. O(n).

questions.q: Why is the complexity O(n) with a nested while?
questions.a: Both pointers only move forward, so in total they move at most 2n steps.

questions.q: Longest run of 1s if you may flip at most k zeros?
questions.a: Keep a window with at most k zeros: when zeros exceed k, move left until a zero leaves the window. Answer is the maximum window length.

questions.q: When does the window method not work?
questions.a: When values can be negative and the condition is about a sum, because shrinking does not necessarily reduce the sum. Use prefix sums + hash map.

questions.q: Find the length of the longest substring with at most k distinct characters.
questions.a:
```
from collections import defaultdict
def longest_k_distinct(s, k):
    cnt, left, best = defaultdict(int), 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        cnt[ch] += 1
        while len(cnt) > k:
            cnt[s[left]] -= 1
            if cnt[s[left]] == 0:
                del cnt[s[left]]
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```

questions.q: Minimum window substring: smallest part of s containing all letters of t.
questions.a: Counter of needed letters, a 'formed' counter of satisfied letters, expand right until formed equals required, then shrink left while still valid, recording the smallest window. O(n).

questions.q: Give a case where sliding window fails.
questions.a: Longest subarray with sum exactly k when numbers can be negative; use prefix sums with a hash map.

questions.q: Why is the answer for 'abba' 2, not 3, in no-repeat substring?
questions.a: When the second 'a' arrives, its previous index is before the window's left edge, so left must not move backwards; the window stays [b, a] length 2.

questions.q: How would you find the busiest 5-minute window in a server log?
questions.a: Sort timestamps, move a left pointer so the window spans at most 5 minutes, and track the maximum number of events in the window.

questions.q: Why is a variable window O(n) despite a nested while?
questions.a: Left and right only move forward, so together they move at most 2n steps.
