questions.q: Why use while and not if for shrinking?
questions.a: One new element may require removing several old ones before the window is valid again.

questions.q: Why does the last-index dictionary jump straight past a duplicate?
questions.a: Everything before the earlier copy of that character must be excluded, so left can move directly beyond it.

questions.q: Why does window fail with negative numbers for sums?
questions.a: Removing a number might increase the sum, so shrinking no longer moves toward validity.

questions.q: Why record the answer after restoring validity (for longest)?
questions.a: Only valid windows count, so measure after the shrink loop.

questions.q: Why check last[ch] >= left?
questions.a: Old entries from before the current window must be ignored; otherwise left could jump backwards.

questions.q: Longest subarray of 1s after deleting one element.
questions.a: Keep a window with at most one zero; answer is the longest window length minus 1.

questions.q: Smallest window containing all characters of t?
questions.a: Counter of needed letters and a 'formed' counter; expand right until satisfied, then shrink left while still satisfied.

questions.q: Array vs linked list - when do you use which?
questions.a: Array (Python list): fast random access O(1), cache friendly, slow insert/delete in the middle O(n). Linked list: O(1) insert/delete when you already hold the node, slow access O(n), extra memory for pointers.

questions.q: How do you delete a node from a singly linked list?
questions.a: Find the node before it (prev) and set prev.next = prev.next.next. For the head, set head = head.next (or use a dummy node).

questions.q: What is a dummy node and why use it?
questions.a: A fake node placed before the head. It makes inserting/deleting at the head the same as anywhere else, and you return dummy.next.

questions.q: How do you find the length of a linked list?
questions.a: Walk with a counter until the node is None. O(n).

questions.q: What is the difference between singly, doubly and circular linked lists?
questions.a: Singly: one pointer (next). Doubly: next and prev. Circular: the last node points back to the first.

questions.q: Why is inserting at the front O(1) for a linked list but O(n) for an array?
questions.a: A linked list only changes two pointers; an array must shift every element to make room.

questions.q: Insert a value in a sorted linked list.
questions.a:
```
def insert_sorted(head, val):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    cur = dummy
    while cur.next and cur.next.val < val:
        cur = cur.next
    cur.next = ListNode(val, cur.next)
    return dummy.next
```

questions.q: What happens if you set cur.next = None while traversing without saving next?
questions.a: The rest of the list becomes unreachable (lost) because the only reference to it was cur.next.

questions.q: How do you implement an LRU cache?
questions.a: A dict from key to node plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency; move a node to the front on access, remove from the tail on eviction. All operations O(1).

questions.q: Why do operating systems use linked lists for free memory blocks?
questions.a: Blocks are allocated and freed in arbitrary places; linking them allows O(1) insertion/removal without moving memory.

questions.q: Why use a linked list at all?
questions.a: Insertion and deletion at a known node change only pointers, with no shifting. It also teaches pointer reasoning.

questions.q: Why not use it for lookup by position?
questions.a: Reaching index i needs i steps: O(n).

questions.q: Why use a dummy node?
questions.a: It removes the special case for the head, so insertion and deletion use the same code everywhere.

questions.q: Why save node.next before changing it?
questions.a: The only reference to the rest of the list is node.next; overwriting it first loses the rest.

questions.q: Why compare nodes with 'is'?
questions.a: Two different nodes can hold equal values. 'is' checks they are the same node object.

questions.q: Why doesn't Python include a built-in linked list?
questions.a: list and deque cover almost every need with better performance and memory layout.

questions.q: Find the length of a linked list.
questions.a:
```
def length(head):
    n = 0
    while head:
        n += 1
        head = head.next
    return n
```

questions.q: What happens if the last node's next points to the head?
questions.a: The list becomes circular; a naive while node: loop never ends.

questions.q: Reverse a linked list iteratively.
questions.a:
```
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev
```

questions.q: What is the time and space complexity?
questions.a: O(n) time and O(1) space for the iterative version. Recursive version uses O(n) stack space.

questions.q: How do you check if a linked list is a palindrome in O(1) space?
questions.a: Find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, compare both halves node by node (optionally restore the list).

questions.q: What goes wrong if you flip the pointer before saving next?
questions.a: You lose the reference to the rest of the list and cannot continue.

questions.q: How do you reverse only a part of the list (positions m to n)?
questions.a: Walk to the node before position m, reverse n - m + 1 nodes with the same prev/cur logic, and reconnect the two ends.

questions.q: Reverse the first k nodes of a linked list.
questions.a:
```
def reverse_first_k(head, k):
    prev, cur = None, head
    for _ in range(k):
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    head.next = cur
    return prev
```

questions.q: Reverse nodes in groups of k.
questions.a: Reverse each group of k with the same loop and reconnect the tail of the previous group to the new head; leave the final group as is if shorter than k.

questions.q: After reversal why is head.next sometimes still pointing to the old second node?
questions.a: Because you forgot to set it; the iterative template sets cur.next = prev, so the old head gets prev = None. If you reuse the old head variable without relinking you can create a cycle.

questions.q: How can you reverse a linked list recursively?
questions.a: Reverse the rest (head.next), then set head.next.next = head and head.next = None, returning the new head.

questions.q: How would you add two numbers stored as linked lists in most-significant-digit order?
questions.a: Reverse both, add with carry as in the reversed-digit problem, then reverse the result (or use stacks).

questions.q: Why three pointers for reversal?
questions.a: prev holds the reversed part, cur the node being flipped, nxt remembers the rest so it is not lost.

questions.q: Why return prev?
questions.a: When cur becomes None, prev is the last real node, the new head.

questions.q: Why is iterative reversal O(1) space but recursive O(n)?
questions.a: Recursion keeps one stack frame per node.

questions.q: Why not copy values into a Python list and rebuild?
questions.a: It works but uses O(n) extra memory and defeats the point of in-place pointer reasoning.

questions.q: Why does the old head end up with next = None?
questions.a: prev starts as None, and the first flip sets head.next = prev.

questions.q: Why is recursion elegant for reversal but risky in Python?
questions.a: Each node adds a frame, so a list of 10^5 nodes exceeds the recursion limit.

questions.q: Reverse a linked list recursively.
questions.a:
```
def rev(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    new_head = rev(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head
```

questions.q: Reverse a sublist between positions m and n.
questions.a: Walk to the node before m, reverse n - m + 1 nodes with the same loop, then reconnect both ends.

questions.q: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
questions.a: Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves 1, fast moves 2. If they meet there is a cycle; if fast hits None there is none. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: How do you find the middle of a linked list?
questions.a: Slow/fast pointers. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle (second middle for even length).

questions.q: How do you find where the cycle begins?
questions.a: After the pointers meet, reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time; the meeting node is the start of the cycle.

questions.q: How do you remove the N-th node from the end?
questions.a: Use a dummy node. Move fast n steps ahead, then move slow and fast together until fast.next is None. Then slow.next = slow.next.next.

questions.q: How do you merge two sorted linked lists?
questions.a: Use a dummy node and a tail pointer. Repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current nodes, then attach the remaining list.

questions.q: Find the length of the cycle.
Why does fast moving by 2 guarantee meeting?
questions.a: Relative speed is 1 node per step inside the loop, so the gap decreases by one each iteration and must reach zero rather than jump over it.

questions.q: Why not move fast by 3?
questions.a: It can still work in some cases, but the gap changes by 2 per step; if the cycle length shares a factor with the gap, fast might skip over slow for several laps. Using 2 guarantees correctness and the simple proof.

questions.q: In a list of 5 nodes with the tail pointing to node 1, what do slow and fast do?
questions.a: They eventually meet inside the cycle, since a cycle exists; the loop terminates when slow is fast.

questions.q: Where else does Floyd's algorithm show up?
questions.a: Detecting repeated states in iterative functions (like 'happy numbers'), finding duplicates in arrays treated as functional graphs and Pollard's rho factorisation.

questions.q: Why must fast and slow meet if a cycle exists?
questions.a: Inside the loop fast gains exactly one node per step on slow, so the gap shrinks by one and must reach zero.

questions.q: Why check fast and fast.next?
questions.a: fast moves two nodes; if fast.next is None, fast.next.next would crash.

questions.q: Why does restarting one pointer at the head find the cycle start?
questions.a: The distance from the head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point to the cycle start going around.

questions.q: Why not just store visited nodes?
questions.a: It works but uses O(n) memory; Floyd uses O(1).

questions.q: Why use a gap of n for 'nth from the end'?
questions.a: When the leading pointer reaches the end, the trailing pointer is exactly n nodes behind.

questions.q: Why not move fast by 3?
questions.a: It can still detect cycles but the correctness argument is less clean and may skip over slow in some cycle lengths.

questions.q: Find the middle of a linked list.
questions.a:
```
def middle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    return slow
```

questions.q: Where do you meet cycle detection outside linked lists?
questions.a: Detecting infinite loops in state machines, repeated states in iterated functions and deadlock-like waits.

questions.q: What is a stack? Give uses.
questions.a: A LIFO collection with push, pop and peek in O(1). Uses: undo/redo, bracket matching, expression evaluation, DFS, function call stack, browser history.

questions.q: How do you check balanced brackets?
How would you implement a queue using two stacks?
questions.a: Push onto an 'inbox' stack. When you need to pop, if the 'outbox' is empty move everything from inbox to outbox (reversing the order) and pop from outbox. Amortised O(1) per operation.

questions.q: How do you get the minimum of a stack in O(1)?
questions.a: Store (value, min so far) pairs, or keep a second stack of minimums.

questions.q: What happens if you pop an empty list?
questions.a: IndexError. Check 'if stack:' before popping.

questions.q: Convert infix to postfix (shunting yard) in outline.
questions.a: Scan tokens; output numbers; push operators on a stack after popping operators of higher or equal precedence to the output; handle '(' by pushing and ')' by popping to the output until '('. At the end pop the rest.

questions.q: What is the final stack after pushing 1, 2, 3, pop, push 4, pop, pop?
questions.a: [1]. Pops remove 3, then 4, then 2.

questions.q: How would you evaluate a normal infix expression with + - * / and parentheses?
questions.a: Two stacks (numbers, operators) with precedence handling, or convert to postfix then evaluate.

questions.q: Why is the call stack a stack?
questions.a: Functions finish in the reverse order that they started: the most recently called function must finish first.

questions.q: How does the browser back button relate to a stack?
questions.a: Visiting a page pushes it; Back pops to the previous page. A second stack supports Forward.

questions.q: Why is a stack LIFO?
questions.a: Many problems resolve the most recent unfinished item first (nested brackets, undo, function calls).

questions.q: Why use a Python list as a stack?
questions.a: append and pop at the end are O(1).

questions.q: Why not use pop(0) for a stack?
questions.a: A stack only touches the end; pop(0) is the queue end and costs O(n).

questions.q: Why check for an empty stack before popping?
questions.a: Popping an empty list raises IndexError.

questions.q: Why is DFS stack-based?
questions.a: It follows one path as deep as possible, then returns to the most recent branch point.

questions.q: Why is a stack better than recursion sometimes?
questions.a: An explicit stack avoids the recursion limit and lets you pause or inspect state.

questions.q: Reverse a string using a stack.
questions.a: Push every character then pop all into a new string. (In Python s[::-1] is shorter.)

questions.q: What is the order when you push 1, 2, 3 and pop twice?
questions.a: 3 then 2; 1 remains.

questions.q: Why should you not use list.pop(0) as a queue?
questions.a: It shifts every remaining element, costing O(n). collections.deque.popleft() is O(1).

questions.q: What is a deque?
questions.a: A double-ended queue with O(1) append and pop at both ends.

questions.q: What is a priority queue and how is it implemented in Python?
questions.a: A queue that always returns the smallest (or highest priority) item first. Python's heapq module (binary min-heap): push and pop are O(log n).

questions.q: How do you make a max-heap with heapq?
questions.a: Store negative values (or use negated priorities) and negate again after popping.

questions.q: How does a circular queue work?
questions.a: A fixed-size array with a front index and a size. Position of the next free slot is (front + size) % capacity; dequeue moves front = (front + 1) % capacity.

questions.q: Implement a queue with a list of two stacks.
questions.a: See the 'Queue Using Two Stacks' problem in the library.

questions.q: Implement a stack using two queues (outline).
questions.a: On push, add to q2, move all items from q1 to q2, then swap the names; pop takes from q1. Push is O(n), pop O(1).

questions.q: What is the difference between a queue and a priority queue?
questions.a: A queue serves by arrival order; a priority queue serves by priority regardless of arrival order.

questions.q: How would you implement a task scheduler that runs the highest-priority task first and FIFO among equals?
questions.a: Heap of (priority, counter, task) where counter is an increasing sequence number to break ties in arrival order.

questions.q: Why do web servers use a queue between request handling and heavy work?
questions.a: It absorbs bursts: requests are enqueued quickly and workers process them at their own pace, preventing overload and enabling retries.

questions.q: Why is deque better than list for queues?
questions.a: popleft is O(1) while list.pop(0) shifts all items.

questions.q: Why use a circular queue?
questions.a: It reuses freed array slots by wrapping indexes, giving a fixed-size queue without wasted space.

questions.q: Why a priority queue instead of sorting repeatedly?
questions.a: A heap gives the next best item in O(log n) after each insert, while re-sorting costs O(n log n).

questions.q: Why does heapq give a min-heap only?
questions.a: That is how the library is written; negate values to simulate a max-heap.

questions.q: Why track size in a circular queue?
questions.a: front == rear is ambiguous (empty or full); a size counter removes the ambiguity.

questions.q: Why not always use a heap when order matters?
questions.a: If you only need arrival order, a deque is simpler and O(1).

questions.q: Implement a queue with two stacks.
questions.a: See the 'Queue Using Two Stacks' problem: push to inbox; when popping with an empty outbox move all items across.

questions.q: Where do message queues help in a web service?
questions.a: They decouple fast request handling from slow work, smooth traffic bursts and allow retries.

questions.q: What is a monotonic stack?
questions.a: A stack whose elements are kept in increasing or decreasing order by popping elements that violate the order when a new element arrives.

questions.q: Solve Next Greater Element in O(n).
questions.a: Scan left to right with a stack of indices waiting for a greater value. For each x pop while nums[stack[-1]] < x and set their answer to x; then push the current index.

questions.q: Why is it O(n) and not O(n^2)?
questions.a: Each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so total work is at most 2n.

questions.q: How would you do daily temperatures?
questions.a: Same as next greater element but store index differences: answer[j] = i - j.

questions.q: What is the largest rectangle in a histogram approach?
questions.a: Keep a stack of increasing bar heights. When a smaller bar arrives, pop taller bars and compute area = height x width where width reaches back to the previous stack element.

questions.q: Compute the stock span for each day (number of consecutive days up to and including today with price <= today).
Trapping rain water with a stack or two pointers.
questions.a: Two pointers keeping left_max and right_max: move the pointer with the smaller max and add max - height. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: next_greater([5, 4, 3, 2, 1]) gives what?
questions.a: [-1, -1, -1, -1, -1]: the list is decreasing, so nothing has a greater element to its right.

questions.q: Why is the algorithm O(n) even with a while loop inside the for loop?
questions.a: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so total pops are bounded by n.

questions.q: Why do compilers use stacks to parse expressions?
questions.a: Nested structure (parentheses, operator precedence) is naturally resolved last-in first-out.

questions.q: Why store indices in the monotonic stack?
questions.a: Indices give both the value (nums[i]) and the distance, which many problems need.

questions.q: Why is the algorithm O(n)?
questions.a: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once.

questions.q: Why pop while the top is smaller?
questions.a: The new element is the answer for every smaller waiting element.

questions.q: Why add a sentinel at the end of a histogram?
questions.a: It forces every remaining bar to be popped and processed.

questions.q: Why not use brute force?
questions.a: It rescans to the right for every element: O(n^2).

questions.q: Why is the stack decreasing for next greater but increasing for next smaller?
questions.a: The waiting elements are those that have not found a bigger (or smaller) partner; keeping the stack ordered the opposite way makes the new element resolve them.

questions.q: Next smaller element for each position.
questions.a: Same template with the comparison reversed: while stack and nums[stack[-1]] > x: res[stack.pop()] = x.

questions.q: next_greater([2, 2, 2]) returns?
questions.a: [-1, -1, -1] with a strict < comparison, because equal values are not greater.

questions.q: What are the parts of a recursive function?
questions.a: A base case that stops the recursion, a recursive case that calls the function with a smaller input, and (usually) a way to combine the results.

questions.q: Why is naive recursive Fibonacci slow?
questions.a: It recomputes the same values exponentially many times (O(2^n)). Memoisation reduces it to O(n).

questions.q: Recursion vs iteration - which is better?
questions.a: Iteration is usually faster and uses O(1) stack. Recursion is clearer for trees, graphs and backtracking. Python has a recursion limit, so deep inputs need loops.

questions.q: What is memoisation?
questions.a: Caching results of function calls by their arguments so repeated calls return instantly.

questions.q: Write a recursive function for the sum of digits.
Compute the n-th Fibonacci number in O(n) with memoisation.
How many calls does fib(5) make without memoisation?
questions.a: 15 calls. The call counts follow calls(n) = calls(n-1) + calls(n-2) + 1.

questions.q: What is a base case and what happens if it is missing or unreachable?
questions.a: It is the case answered without recursion. If missing, the recursion never stops and Python raises RecursionError.

questions.q: Convert a recursive DFS into an iterative one.
questions.a: Use an explicit stack; push the start; pop a node, process it and push unvisited neighbours.

questions.q: How does an operating system list all files under a folder?
questions.a: A recursive walk: for each entry, if it is a folder recurse into it; if it is a file record it.

questions.q: Why does naive Fibonacci take exponential time?
questions.a: It recomputes the same subproblems over and over (fib(3) many times).

questions.q: Why add memoisation?
questions.a: Each distinct n is computed once, reducing the work to O(n).

questions.q: Why does Python limit recursion depth?
questions.a: To protect the interpreter from running out of memory in endless recursion.

questions.q: Why do recursion and induction feel alike?
questions.a: Both solve the base case and then show that solving the smaller case lets you solve the bigger one.

questions.q: Why not convert every recursion to a loop?
questions.a: Some problems (trees, backtracking) are far clearer recursively.

questions.q: Why does a tail call not help in Python?
questions.a: CPython does not optimise tail calls, so each call still uses a stack frame.

questions.q: Write recursion to compute the sum of a list.
How many calls does fact(5) make?
questions.a: 5 calls (n = 5, 4, 3, 2, 1) when the base case is n <= 1.

questions.q: Explain backtracking.
questions.a: Build a solution step by step. At each step choose, recurse, then undo the choice. Prune branches that cannot lead to a valid answer.

questions.q: Generate all subsets of a list.
questions.a:
```
def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    def go(start):
        res.append(path[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])
            go(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    go(0)
    return res
```

questions.q: Why must you copy the path before storing it?
questions.a: path is a single list that keeps changing. If you store the list itself, all stored answers end up pointing to the same final (empty) list.

questions.q: How do you avoid duplicate subsets when the input has duplicates?
questions.a: Sort the input and skip nums[i] if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1].

questions.q: Time complexity of generating all permutations?
questions.a: O(n x n!). There are n! permutations and each takes O(n) to copy.

questions.q: What is pruning?
questions.a: Stopping a branch early when it cannot possibly produce a valid solution (for example the remaining sum is already negative).

questions.q: Generate all combinations of k numbers from 1..n.
questions.a:
```
def combine(n, k):
    res, path = [], []
    def go(start):
        if len(path) == k:
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, n + 1):
            path.append(i)
            go(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    go(1)
    return res
```

questions.q: Why does res.append(path) produce a list of empty lists at the end?
questions.a: All entries reference the same list object that is emptied by backtracking. Append a copy: path[:].

questions.q: Solve a Sudoku.
questions.a: Backtrack on empty cells: try digits 1-9 that do not conflict in row, column and box; recurse; undo on failure. Track used digits in sets for O(1) checks.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of generating all subsets?
questions.a: O(n x 2^n): there are 2^n subsets and copying each takes up to O(n).

questions.q: Where might a company use backtracking?
questions.a: Shift scheduling, exam timetables, itinerary planning and any problem with many interacting constraints.

questions.q: Why undo (pop) after each recursive call?
questions.a: The shared path must return to its previous state before the next option is tried.

questions.q: Why store path[:] and not path?
questions.a: path keeps changing; a copy freezes the current answer.

questions.q: Why use a start index in subsets?
questions.a: It ensures each subset is built in increasing order so none is generated twice.

questions.q: Why prune?
questions.a: Cutting branches that cannot succeed avoids exploring huge parts of the search space.

questions.q: Why sort the input for duplicate handling?
questions.a: Equal values become adjacent, so a simple 'skip if equal to the previous' rule removes duplicate subsets.

questions.q: Why is backtracking only for small n?
questions.a: The number of results grows as 2^n or n!, which becomes impossible beyond about n = 20 or 10.

questions.q: Generate all combinations of k numbers from 1..n.
questions.a: Backtrack with a start index; record the path when its length equals k.

questions.q: How would you count subsets with sum k without listing them?
questions.a: Use dynamic programming (subset-sum) instead of backtracking.

questions.q: Explain the N-Queens algorithm.
questions.a: Place queens row by row. For each row try each column; skip squares attacked via column or diagonal (checked with sets); place, recurse, remove (backtrack). Count or collect solutions when all rows are filled.

questions.q: How do you check diagonals in constant time?
questions.a: Cells on the same '/' diagonal share row + col, cells on the same '\' diagonal share row - col. Keep sets of those values.

questions.q: How many solutions does 8-Queens have?
questions.a: 92 (12 if you count rotations and reflections as the same).

questions.q: What is the time complexity?
questions.a: Roughly O(n!) in the worst case, far smaller in practice due to pruning.

questions.q: Name another problem solved the same way.
questions.a: Sudoku solver, word search in a grid, graph colouring, rat in a maze.

questions.q: Return all N-Queens boards as lists of strings.
questions.a: Record the column of each row in a list; at the end build strings with 'Q' at the column and '.' elsewhere, e.g. ['.Q..', '...Q', ...].

questions.q: How do you detect diagonal conflicts in O(1)?
questions.a: Cells on the same diagonal share r - c and on the other diagonal share r + c; keep sets of used values.

questions.q: How could you speed it up?
questions.a: Use bit masks for columns and both diagonals, or exploit symmetry by solving only half of the first row.

questions.q: How many solutions does 6-Queens have?
Is N-Queens used in practice?
questions.a: As a benchmark for constraint solvers and as a model of resource placement where items must not interfere.

questions.q: Why one queen per row?
questions.a: Two queens in a row attack each other, so every row has exactly one.

questions.q: Why use three sets for conflicts?
questions.a: Columns, row-col diagonals and row+col diagonals can then be checked in O(1).

questions.q: Why is pruning crucial?
questions.a: Without it the search tries n^n placements; with it only safe partial boards are expanded.

questions.q: Why does n = 2 and 3 have no solution?
questions.a: There is no way to place the queens without attacks on such small boards.

questions.q: Why backtrack instead of trying placements randomly?
questions.a: Systematic search guarantees you find every solution or prove none exists.

questions.q: Why not use brute force over all C(n^2, n) placements?
questions.a: For n = 8 that is about 4.4 billion boards; backtracking visits only a few thousand.

questions.q: Return one solution board for n queens, or an empty list.
questions.a: Backtrack and stop at the first complete placement, then render columns as rows of strings.

questions.q: Where do 'no two conflicting' placements appear in practice?
questions.a: Scheduling, seating charts, frequency assignment and layout problems where items must not clash.

questions.q: What are the tree traversals and their orders?
questions.a: Inorder: left, node, right. Preorder: node, left, right. Postorder: left, right, node. Level order: level by level with a queue.

questions.q: What does inorder traversal of a BST give?
questions.a: The values in sorted ascending order.

questions.q: How do you find the height of a binary tree?
questions.a: height(node) = 0 if None else 1 + max(height(left), height(right)). O(n).

questions.q: Difference between depth and height?
questions.a: Depth is measured from the root down to a node; height is measured from a node down to its deepest leaf.

questions.q: How do you do level order traversal?
questions.a: Use a queue. Process the number of nodes currently in the queue as one level and add their children for the next level.

questions.q: What is the space complexity of recursive DFS on a tree?
questions.a: O(h) for the call stack, where h is the height.

questions.q: Iterative inorder traversal.
questions.a:
```
def inorder(root):
    res, st, cur = [], [], root
    while st or cur:
        while cur:
            st.append(cur)
            cur = cur.left
        cur = st.pop()
        res.append(cur.val)
        cur = cur.right
    return res
```

questions.q: For the tree 1 with children 2 and 3, what are the preorder, inorder, postorder?
questions.a: Preorder 1 2 3, inorder 2 1 3, postorder 2 3 1.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h (counting edges)?
Reconstruct a tree from preorder and inorder lists.
questions.a: The first preorder value is the root; find it in inorder to split left and right subtrees and recurse. Use a dict from value to inorder index for O(n).

questions.q: How does a browser use a tree?
questions.a: It parses HTML into a DOM tree; styling and layout walk the tree, and events bubble up from child to parent.

questions.q: Why use a tree instead of a list for hierarchies?
questions.a: A list cannot express 'belongs to'. A tree gives every item one parent and shows containment directly.

questions.q: Why is tree recursion so short?
questions.a: Every subtree is itself a tree, so one function handles the node and trusts recursive calls for the children.

questions.q: Why are there three DFS orders?
questions.a: They differ in when the node is processed: before children (copy), between children (sorted order in a BST), after children (delete or evaluate).

questions.q: Why does BFS need a queue?
questions.a: It must serve the oldest discovered node first to go level by level.

questions.q: Why can recursion fail on a skewed tree?
questions.a: Depth equals the number of nodes, which can exceed Python's recursion limit. Use an iterative traversal.

questions.q: Why not store a tree as a list of lists?
questions.a: You can (heaps do, using index arithmetic), but for general trees node objects are clearer.

questions.q: Count the leaf nodes of a binary tree.
How many nodes does a full binary tree of height 3 (edges) have?
What is a binary search tree?
questions.a: A binary tree where for every node, all values in the left subtree are smaller and all values in the right subtree are larger.

questions.q: Time complexity of BST operations?
questions.a: O(h): O(log n) when balanced and O(n) when skewed.

questions.q: How do you validate a BST?
questions.a: Recurse with the allowed range: left child must be within (low, node.val) and right child within (node.val, high). Checking only the parent is wrong.

questions.q: How do you delete a node with two children?
questions.a: Replace its value with its inorder successor (smallest in the right subtree) and then delete that successor node.

questions.q: How do you find the k-th smallest element in a BST?
questions.a: Do an inorder traversal and stop at the k-th visited node (iterative stack solution is O(h + k)).

questions.q: Why can a BST become O(n)?
questions.a: If values are inserted in sorted order the tree becomes a chain.

questions.q: Find the lowest common ancestor in a BST.
Why can a BST degrade to O(n)?
questions.a: Inserting sorted data produces a one-sided chain, so height is n and operations walk the whole chain. Self-balancing trees fix this.

questions.q: Convert a sorted array to a height-balanced BST.
questions.a: Pick the middle element as root and recursively build left and right subtrees from the two halves. O(n).

questions.q: Is the tree [5, 1, 4, None, None, 3, 6] a valid BST?
questions.a: No. Node 3 is in the right subtree of 5 but 3 < 5, violating the ancestor rule.

questions.q: How does a database answer a range query using a tree?
questions.a: It searches to the first key in range (O(log n)) and then walks in order through the leaves until the end of the range.

questions.q: Why does a BST give sorted order by inorder traversal?
questions.a: Everything on the left is smaller and on the right larger, so left, node, right visits values in ascending order.

questions.q: Why can a BST be slow?
questions.a: Inserting sorted data creates a chain of height n, so operations take O(n).

questions.q: Why validate with bounds instead of parent-child checks?
questions.a: A node must respect ALL its ancestors, not only its parent.

questions.q: Why replace a two-child node by its inorder successor?
questions.a: The successor is the next larger value; swapping it in keeps the ordering valid.

questions.q: Why not use a BST when only exact lookups are needed?
questions.a: A hash table does exact lookups in O(1) average.

questions.q: Why do databases use B-trees rather than binary search trees?
questions.a: B-trees have many keys per node, so they are shallower and read fewer disk blocks.

questions.q: Insert a value into a BST iteratively.
questions.a: Walk down comparing with each node and attach a new node at the first empty child spot.

questions.q: Find the inorder successor of a node in a BST.
questions.a: If it has a right child, take that subtree's leftmost node; otherwise it is the nearest ancestor for which the node is in the left subtree.

questions.q: How do you check if a tree is height balanced efficiently?
questions.a: Compute heights bottom-up. A helper returns the height or -1 when unbalanced. This is O(n) instead of calling height at every node (O(n^2)).

questions.q: What is the diameter of a binary tree and how do you compute it?
questions.a: The number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. For each node the longest path through it is height(left) + height(right); take the maximum while computing heights. O(n).

questions.q: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes.
questions.a: Recurse: if node is None or equals a target return node; get left and right answers; if both are non-null return node; else return whichever is non-null.

questions.q: How do you check if a tree is symmetric?
questions.a: Compare the left and right subtrees as mirrors: left.left with right.right and left.right with right.left, recursively.

questions.q: How do you check if a root-to-leaf path has a given sum?
questions.a: Subtract each node's value from the target while going down; at a leaf the remaining target must be 0.

questions.q: Maximum path sum in a binary tree (path may start and end anywhere).
What does 'post-order information passing' mean?
questions.a: Each node computes its result after its children and returns it to its parent, combining the children's results.

questions.q: Check if a tree is symmetric.
questions.a: Compare left and right subtrees as mirrors recursively: a.left with b.right and a.right with b.left.

questions.q: Why is calling height() in every node of is_balanced slow?
questions.a: It re-walks subtrees repeatedly: O(n^2) for a skewed tree. Return height from one pass with -1 for unbalanced.

questions.q: Write BFS.
questions.a:
```
from collections import deque
def bfs(graph, start):
    seen, order = {start}, []
    q = deque([start])
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            if v not in seen:
                seen.add(v)
                q.append(v)
    return order
```

questions.a:
```
def dfs(graph, start):
    seen, stack, order = set(), [start], []
    while stack:
        u = stack.pop()
        if u in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(u)
        order.append(u)
        stack.extend(reversed(graph[u]))
    return order
```

What is a trie and what is it used for?

questions.q: Why do we need an end-of-word flag?
questions.a: To distinguish stored words from mere prefixes of other words.

questions.q: Trie vs hash set of words?
questions.a: A set gives O(L) exact search but cannot do prefix queries efficiently. A trie supports prefix queries and ordered traversal.

questions.q: How would you find all words with a given prefix?

Tell me about your approach to solving a coding problem.
questions.a: I clarify the problem and constraints, work through examples, think of a simple correct solution first, then improve it using the right data structure or technique. I state the time and space complexity, code carefully, and dry-run my code on the sample and an edge case before finishing.

questions.q: How do you choose between a list, a set and a dictionary?
questions.a: List: ordered items accessed by position. Set: unique items and fast membership checks. Dictionary: map from a key to a value for fast lookup or counting.

questions.q: What is the difference between time complexity and space complexity?
questions.a: Time complexity measures how the number of steps grows with input size. Space complexity measures how the extra memory grows.

questions.q: How do you test your code when no tests are given?
questions.a: I test the sample, an empty or minimal input, an input with all equal elements, negative numbers, the largest input, and compare with a simple brute force on small random inputs.

questions.q: What would you do if your solution is too slow?
questions.a: Re-check the constraints, find repeated work, and replace it: hashing for lookups, sorting plus two pointers, prefix sums for ranges, binary search for sorted data, heap for repeated min/max, DP for repeated subproblems.

questions.q: Why is Python a good language for coding rounds, and what are its pitfalls?
questions.a: It is short and readable with powerful built-ins (Counter, heapq, bisect, sorted). Pitfalls: slower than C++/Java for huge loops, recursion limit around 1000, mutable default arguments and shallow copies of lists.

questions.q: Explain mutable vs immutable types in Python.
questions.a: Mutable objects (list, dict, set) can change in place; immutable ones (int, str, tuple) cannot. Immutable objects are hashable and safe as dictionary keys.

questions.q: What is the difference between a shallow and a deep copy?
questions.a: Shallow copy copies only the outer container; inner objects are shared. Deep copy copies everything recursively.

questions.q: What are Python generators and why are they useful?
questions.a: Functions using yield that produce items one at a time without storing everything, saving memory for large data.

questions.q: What does the 'with' statement do?
questions.a: It manages a resource such as a file: it makes sure the file is closed even if an error happens.

questions.q: What is a lambda function?
questions.a: A small anonymous function written in one line, for example key=lambda x: x[1].

questions.q: What is the difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression?
questions.a: A list comprehension [..] builds the whole list in memory; a generator expression (..) produces items lazily one by one.

questions.q: What is the GIL?
questions.a: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time in CPython, so threads do not speed up CPU-bound code (use multiprocessing).

questions.q: What are *args and **kwargs?
questions.a: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.

questions.q: What are Python's main built-in data structures and when do you use each?
questions.a: list: ordered, changeable sequence. tuple: ordered, fixed sequence (can be a dict key). dict: key to value mapping with fast lookup. set: unique items with fast membership. str: immutable text. Choose by what you need to do most: index (list), look up by key (dict), test membership (set), keep fixed records (tuple).

questions.q: Explain the difference between a list and a generator.
questions.a: A list stores all items in memory. A generator produces items one at a time when asked (using yield or a generator expression) and uses almost no memory. Use generators for large or infinite streams.

questions.q: What is a decorator?
questions.a: A function that takes another function and returns a new function that adds behaviour (logging, timing, caching). The @decorator syntax is shorthand for f = decorator(f). functools.lru_cache is a decorator.

questions.q: What are classes and objects? Explain __init__ and self.
questions.a: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance. __init__ runs when an object is created to set up its attributes. self is the object the method is being called on.

questions.q: What is inheritance and what is method overriding?
questions.a: Inheritance lets a class reuse another class's attributes and methods. Overriding means a subclass defines a method with the same name to change its behaviour; super() calls the parent version.

questions.q: Explain exceptions: try, except, else, finally.
questions.a: try holds code that may fail; except handles a specific error; else runs if no error happened; finally always runs (cleanup). Catch specific exceptions, not a bare except.

questions.q: What is the difference between == and is, and between copy and deepcopy?
questions.a: == compares values; is compares identity. copy makes a shallow copy (inner objects shared); deepcopy copies everything recursively.

questions.q: What are dunder (magic) methods?
questions.a: Special methods with double underscores that Python calls for you: __init__ (create), __str__/__repr__ (print), __len__ (len()), __eq__ (==), __lt__ (<), __hash__ (hashing).

questions.q: What does the 'with' statement do and why use it?
questions.a: It runs setup and cleanup automatically (a context manager). With open(...) the file is closed even if an error occurs.

questions.q: How does Python pass arguments to functions?
questions.a: Arguments are references to objects (pass by object reference). Mutating a mutable argument inside a function changes the caller's object; rebinding the parameter name does not.

questions.q: What are *args and **kwargs?
questions.a: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict.

questions.q: What are list comprehensions and when should you avoid them?
questions.a: A compact way to build a list from a loop. Avoid them when the logic is long or has side effects; use a normal loop for readability.

questions.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
questions.a: A process is a running program with its own memory. A thread is a lightweight unit of execution inside a process that shares the process's memory. Threads are cheaper to create but need care with shared data.

questions.q: What are stack memory and heap memory?
questions.a: Stack memory holds function call frames and local variables, allocated and freed automatically. Heap memory holds dynamically created objects whose lifetime is managed explicitly or by a garbage collector.

questions.q: Compiled vs interpreted languages?
questions.a: Compiled languages are translated to machine code before running (e.g. C). Interpreted languages are executed by an interpreter (e.g. Python); CPython compiles to bytecode that a virtual machine runs.

questions.q: What is a database index and why does it help?
questions.a: A separate sorted structure (often a B-tree) that lets the database find rows by a column without scanning the whole table, trading extra space and slower writes for fast reads.

questions.q: Explain SQL joins briefly.
questions.a: INNER JOIN returns rows with matching keys in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matches from the right (NULL when none). RIGHT JOIN is the mirror; FULL JOIN returns all rows from both.

questions.q: What does ACID mean in databases?
questions.a: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules always hold), Isolation (transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes).

questions.q: What happens when you type a URL in a browser (short version)?
questions.a: The browser resolves the domain to an IP via DNS, opens a TCP (and TLS) connection, sends an HTTP request, receives the response and renders the HTML, loading further resources.

questions.q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
questions.a: TCP is connection-based and reliable (ordered, retransmits lost data) - used for web and email. UDP is connectionless and faster but unreliable - used for streaming and games.

questions.q: Why does recursion cost more memory than a loop?
questions.a: Each recursive call pushes a stack frame (memory and time). Iteration reuses the same frame, so it uses O(1) extra stack.

questions.q: What is Big-O and why do we use it?
questions.a: A way to describe how running time or memory grows with input size, ignoring constants, so algorithms can be compared independently of hardware.

questions.q: Walk me through how you would solve: 'find two numbers in a list that add to a target'.
questions.a: I would clarify: sorted or not, duplicates, indices or values, one answer or all. Then say brute force: two loops, O(n^2). Then improve: one pass with a dictionary storing seen values; check target - x before inserting x. O(n) time and O(n) space. I would test [2,7,11,15] with 9, [3,3] with 6 and an empty list.

questions.q: How do you decide between a hash map and sorting for a problem?
questions.a: If I only need membership, counts or pairs and order does not matter, a hash map gives O(n). If I need order, ranges, nearest values or O(1) extra space, sorting (then two pointers or binary search) is better.

questions.q: What do you do when you cannot think of the optimal solution?
questions.a: I state a correct brute force and its complexity, find the repeated work, and try standard tools: hashing, sorting, two pointers, prefix sums, heap, binary search, DP. Starting from brute force always gives a base to improve.

questions.q: How do you verify your solution without a judge?
questions.a: Dry-run the sample by hand, test an empty/minimal input, a single element, duplicates, negatives and the largest input size mentally, and compare against a brute force on small random inputs if time permits.

questions.q: How do you explain your solution to the interviewer?
questions.a: Restate the problem, describe the idea in plain words, walk through an example, state complexity and edge cases, then code. Narrating decisions ('I use a set because membership is O(1)') shows understanding.

questions.q: How do you manage time in a 60-minute coding test with 3 problems?
questions.a: Skim all, solve the easiest first, time-box each problem, submit a working version early, return to improve, and keep the last minutes for re-testing edge cases.
