questions.q: What problem does a Fenwick tree (BIT) solve?
questions.a: Point updates and prefix-sum queries in O(log n) with O(n) memory and a very small constant, using lowbit (i & -i) to jump between nodes.

questions.q: When would you choose a segment tree over a Fenwick tree?
questions.a: When the operation is not invertible (min, max, gcd) or you need range updates with lazy propagation. A Fenwick tree needs an invertible operation for range queries.

questions.q: What is a sparse table and what are its limits?
questions.a: A table of answers for ranges of length 2^k, built in O(n log n), giving O(1) queries for idempotent operations like min and max. It does not support updates.

questions.q: Explain lazy propagation.
questions.a: Store pending updates on internal nodes and push them to children only when a later operation needs to descend, so range updates and range queries both stay O(log n).

questions.q: How do AVL trees stay balanced?
questions.a: Each node's subtree heights differ by at most one; insertions and deletions fix violations with single or double rotations, giving O(log n) operations.

questions.q: How do you implement an LFU cache in O(1)?
questions.a: A hash map from key to node plus a map from frequency to an ordered list of keys, with a tracked minimum frequency that is updated on every access and eviction.

questions.q: What is a monotonic deque used for?
questions.a: Sliding window maximum or minimum in O(n): keep indexes whose values are monotonic, pop dominated elements from the back and expired ones from the front.

questions.q: Compare a hash table with a balanced BST.
questions.a: Hash tables give O(1) average lookups but no ordering. Balanced BSTs give O(log n) with ordered traversal, predecessor/successor and range queries.

questions.q: How do you answer 'number of elements less than x in a range' with updates?
questions.a: Offline with a Fenwick tree and coordinate compression, a merge sort tree, a persistent segment tree, or sqrt decomposition depending on constraints.

questions.q: What is a persistent data structure?
questions.a: One that preserves earlier versions after updates, usually by path copying so each update adds O(log n) new nodes while old roots remain valid.

questions.q: Why do skip lists appear in practice?
questions.a: They give expected O(log n) ordered operations with simple code and good concurrency properties; Redis sorted sets use them.

questions.q: What is amortised O(1) for union-find and what makes it so fast?
questions.a: With union by rank (or size) and path compression, any sequence of m operations costs O(m alpha(n)), where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function, below 5 for practical n.

questions.q: What is a B-tree and why do databases use it?
questions.a: A balanced multiway tree with large nodes sized to disk pages; the high fan-out keeps the tree very shallow, minimising disk reads.

questions.q: How does a bloom filter work and what are its error properties?
questions.a: k hash functions set bits in a bit array; a query reports present only if all k bits are set. It has false positives but no false negatives and cannot delete (without counting variants).

questions.q: BFS versus DFS: when do you use each?
questions.a: BFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs and level order; DFS for cycle detection, topological order, components and backtracking.

questions.q: Why can't Dijkstra handle negative edges?
questions.a: It finalises a node when popped assuming no later path can be shorter, which a negative edge can violate. Use Bellman-Ford instead.

questions.q: What is the complexity of Dijkstra with a binary heap?
questions.a: O((V + E) log V) in the lazy-deletion form.

questions.q: Explain Bellman-Ford and negative cycles.
questions.a: Relax every edge V - 1 times. If another pass still improves a distance, a negative cycle is reachable.

questions.q: Floyd-Warshall: what does it compute and what is the loop order?
questions.a: All-pairs shortest paths in O(V^3). The intermediate vertex k must be the outermost loop.

questions.q: Kruskal versus Prim?
questions.a: Kruskal sorts edges and joins components with union-find (good for sparse graphs). Prim grows a tree from a start node with a heap (good for dense graphs). Both are O(E log V).

questions.q: How do you find strongly connected components?
questions.a: Tarjan's algorithm (low-link values in one DFS) or Kosaraju's (DFS finishing order, then DFS on the reversed graph). Both O(V + E).

questions.q: How do you test if a graph is bipartite?
questions.a: BFS or DFS two-colouring; a conflict on an edge means an odd cycle, so it is not bipartite.

questions.q: What are bridges and articulation points?
questions.a: A bridge is an edge, and an articulation point a vertex, whose removal disconnects the graph. Found with DFS discovery times and low-link values in O(V + E).

questions.q: What is A* and when is it optimal?
questions.a: Best-first search ordered by g + h, where h estimates the remaining cost. It is optimal with an admissible heuristic (never overestimates), and consistent heuristics avoid reopening nodes.

questions.q: How does max flow relate to min cut?
questions.a: The max-flow min-cut theorem: the maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut. Ford-Fulkerson with BFS (Edmonds-Karp) runs in O(V E^2).

questions.q: How is bipartite matching solved?
questions.a: As a max-flow problem or with Hopcroft-Karp in O(E sqrt V); Konig's theorem links the maximum matching to the minimum vertex cover in bipartite graphs.

questions.q: How do you solve 2-SAT?
questions.a: Build the implication graph, compute SCCs; the formula is unsatisfiable iff a variable and its negation share a component, and a topological order yields an assignment.

questions.q: How would you find the shortest path with at most k edges?
questions.a: Bellman-Ford limited to k rounds (using a copy of the previous distances) or BFS/Dijkstra on a state graph of (node, edges used).

questions.q: How do you detect a cycle in a directed versus undirected graph?
questions.a: Directed: DFS with three colours or Kahn's algorithm. Undirected: DFS/BFS that sees a visited node other than its parent, or union-find.

questions.q: How do you recognise a DP problem?
questions.a: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure: a recursive solution that recomputes the same states, where the best answer builds from best answers to smaller states.

questions.q: Top-down versus bottom-up DP?
questions.a: Top-down memoises recursion and computes only needed states; bottom-up fills a table in dependency order, avoiding recursion depth and enabling space optimisation.

questions.q: Solve 0/1 knapsack and give its complexity.
questions.a: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt] + val), iterating w downward for 0/1. O(nW) time, O(W) space; it is pseudo-polynomial.

questions.q: Why iterate capacity downward in 0/1 knapsack but upward for unbounded?
questions.a: Downward prevents reusing an item within the same pass; upward intentionally allows reusing the same item.

questions.q: Longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n)?
questions.a: Keep tails[k], the smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1, and binary search each element's position.

questions.q: Define edit distance DP.
questions.a: dp[i][j] is the cost to convert the first i characters to the first j: equal characters copy dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).

questions.q: How do you reconstruct the answer, not only its value?
questions.a: Store the choice (parent pointer) at each state, or walk backwards through the table checking which transition produced the value.

questions.q: Interval DP: describe the pattern.
questions.a: dp[l][r] combines dp over split points k in [l, r), iterating by increasing length. Examples: matrix chain, burst balloons, optimal BST.

questions.q: When do you use bitmask DP?
questions.a: When n is small (about 20) and the state is the subset of items used, as in TSP in O(2^n n^2), assignment problems and partitioning.

questions.q: Explain digit DP.
questions.a: Count numbers up to N with a property by processing digits left to right with state (position, tight, extra info like sum or last digit), memoising when not tight.

questions.q: What is the knapsack optimisation for large weights but small values?
questions.a: Swap the dimensions: dp[value] = minimum weight, giving O(n sum of values), the basis of the FPTAS.

questions.q: How do convex hull trick and divide-and-conquer optimisation speed up DP?
questions.a: When transitions are lines or satisfy monotone optimal split points, you can reduce O(n^2) transitions to O(n log n) or O(n).

questions.q: Tree DP: how is it structured?
questions.a: Compute states for children first (post-order) and combine them, e.g. maximum independent set with dp[v][taken] or rerooting to get answers for every root.

questions.q: Why is the coin change count different from the minimum coins DP?
questions.a: Counting combinations loops over coins outside and amounts inside (order ignored); counting sequences swaps the loops. Minimum uses min instead of sum.

questions.q: Naive pattern matching complexity and when it is bad?
questions.a: O(n m) worst case, such as aaaa...ab against aaa...a, because comparisons restart at every position.

questions.q: What is a trie and what are its operations' costs?
questions.a: A prefix tree with insert, search and prefix queries in O(length) regardless of dictionary size, at the cost of memory.

questions.q: How do you check whether one string is a rotation of another?
questions.a: Same length and the second occurs inside the first concatenated with itself.

questions.q: Explain the KMP prefix function.
questions.a: pi[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also a suffix. On a mismatch the matcher falls back to pi[k - 1] instead of restarting, giving O(n + m).

questions.q: Why is KMP linear?
questions.a: The fallback pointer only moves forward one step per character and each fallback decreases it, so total moves are bounded by 2n.

questions.q: What does the Z array give?
questions.a: z[i] is the longest common prefix of s and s[i:]; pattern matching on P + '$' + T finds matches where z equals |P|.

questions.q: How does Rabin-Karp work and what is its failure mode?
questions.a: It compares rolling hashes of windows with the pattern hash, verifying equal hashes. Collisions or adversarial inputs can degrade it to O(n m); use a large modulus and random base.

questions.q: How do you find the smallest repeating period of a string?
questions.a: Take p = n - pi[n - 1]; if p divides n then p is the period, otherwise the string is primitive (period n).

questions.q: Manacher's algorithm in one paragraph.
questions.a: Insert separators, keep the centre and right edge of the rightmost palindrome, and initialise the radius at i from its mirror, then expand. Each expansion moves the right edge, so O(n) overall.

questions.q: What is Aho-Corasick and where is it used?
questions.a: A trie with failure links that finds all occurrences of many patterns in a single pass, O(n + total pattern length + matches). Used in malware scanners and filters.

questions.q: What is a suffix array and what can you do with it?
questions.a: The sorted order of all suffixes. With an LCP array it supports substring search by binary search, longest repeated substring, distinct substring counting and longest common substring.

questions.q: Suffix array versus suffix tree versus suffix automaton?
questions.a: All index all substrings. Suffix trees are the most flexible but memory heavy; suffix arrays are compact and cache friendly; suffix automata are small and build online in linear time.

questions.q: How do you count distinct substrings?
questions.a: n(n + 1)/2 minus the sum of the LCP array of the suffix array.

questions.q: How do you find the shortest palindrome by prepending characters?
questions.a: Compute the prefix function of s + '#' + reverse(s); the last value is the longest palindromic prefix, and the rest of the reversed string is prepended.

questions.q: How do you compute gcd and lcm?
questions.a: Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), O(log). lcm = a / gcd * b, dividing first to limit overflow.

questions.q: How do you test primality quickly?
questions.a: Trial division to sqrt(n) for small n, a sieve for many queries, and Miller-Rabin for very large numbers.

questions.q: How do you check if n is a power of two?
Why use 10^9 + 7 as a modulus?
questions.a: It is a prime below 2^30, so products fit in 64 bits and every non-zero residue has a modular inverse by Fermat's little theorem.

questions.q: How do you compute a^b mod m efficiently?
questions.a: Binary exponentiation: square the base and multiply when the bit is set, O(log b). Python: pow(a, b, m).

questions.q: How do you divide modulo a prime?
questions.a: Multiply by the modular inverse, b^(p - 2) mod p, or pow(b, -1, p) in Python 3.8+.

questions.q: How do you compute nCr mod p for many queries?
questions.a: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to n, then answer in O(1).

questions.q: Explain the sieve of Eratosthenes.
questions.a: Mark multiples of each prime starting from p^2 as composite. O(n log log n) time and O(n) memory.

questions.q: What is the expected number of fixed points of a random permutation?
questions.a: 1, by linearity of expectation: n indicators each with probability 1/n.

questions.q: State the Chinese remainder theorem.
questions.a: For pairwise coprime moduli, x = r_i (mod m_i) has a unique solution modulo the product, found by combining congruences with modular inverses.

questions.q: How do you compute Fibonacci(n) for huge n?
questions.a: Matrix exponentiation of [[1,1],[1,0]] in O(log n) 2x2 multiplications, or fast doubling.

questions.q: What is Euler's totient and its use?
questions.a: phi(n) counts integers up to n coprime to n. Euler's theorem gives a^phi(n) = 1 (mod n) for coprime a, used for inverses and reducing exponents.

questions.q: How do you uniformly sample one item from a stream of unknown length?
questions.a: Reservoir sampling: replace the current pick with the i-th item with probability 1/i.

questions.q: Why is a naive shuffle that swaps each element with a random index biased?
questions.a: It generates n^n equally likely outcomes, which cannot divide evenly into n! permutations. Fisher-Yates swaps with a random later index and is uniform.

questions.q: Difference between O, Omega and Theta?
questions.a: Upper bound, lower bound, and tight bound. They are independent of best/worst/average case.

questions.q: What is the complexity of nested loops where the inner runs i times?
questions.a: Sum of i from 1 to n is n(n + 1)/2, which is Theta(n^2).

questions.q: What is amortised analysis?
questions.a: Averaging the cost over a worst-case sequence of operations, e.g. dynamic array append is O(1) amortised although a resize costs O(n).

questions.q: State the Master theorem.
questions.a: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): compare f with n^(log_b a). If f is polynomially smaller the answer is n^(log_b a); if equal, n^(log_b a) log n; if polynomially larger (with regularity), f(n).

questions.q: Why do comparison sorts need Omega(n log n)?
questions.a: A decision tree with n! leaves has height at least log2(n!), which is Theta(n log n).

questions.q: What is the difference between P and NP?
questions.a: P can be solved in polynomial time; NP can be verified in polynomial time given a certificate. P is a subset of NP; whether they are equal is open.

questions.q: What does NP-complete mean?
questions.a: A problem in NP to which every problem in NP reduces in polynomial time.

questions.q: Name some NP-complete problems.
questions.a: SAT, 3-SAT, clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, subset sum, graph colouring, travelling salesman (decision).

questions.q: What is pseudo-polynomial time?
questions.a: Polynomial in the numeric value of the input rather than its bit length, like knapsack DP O(nW). The problem remains weakly NP-hard.

questions.q: How do you prove a problem is NP-hard?
questions.a: Reduce a known NP-hard problem to it in polynomial time, so a fast algorithm for the new problem would solve the known one.

questions.q: What strategies exist for NP-hard problems in practice?
questions.a: Exact search with pruning, DP over small parameters, approximation algorithms with guarantees, heuristics and local search, and exploiting special structure.

questions.q: Give an approximation algorithm and its guarantee.
questions.a: Vertex cover: take both endpoints of each edge in a maximal matching, giving at most twice the optimum.

questions.q: Why is the 2-SAT problem in P but 3-SAT NP-complete?
questions.a: 2-SAT reduces to reachability in an implication graph, solved by SCCs in linear time; no such structure exists for three-literal clauses.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of recursive Fibonacci and how do you improve it?
questions.a: Exponential, about 1.618^n. Memoisation or iteration makes it O(n), matrix exponentiation O(log n).

questions.q: Two Sum: what are the approaches?
questions.a: Hash map of complement values in O(n) time; or sort and use two pointers in O(n log n) if indexes are not needed.

questions.q: How do you reverse a linked list?
questions.a: Iterate keeping prev, curr and next, flipping each pointer. O(n) time, O(1) space; recursion uses O(n) stack.

questions.q: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
questions.a: Floyd's tortoise and hare: a fast and a slow pointer meet inside a cycle. To find the start, reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time.

questions.q: Valid parentheses?
questions.a: Use a stack: push openers, and each closer must match the top.

questions.q: Subarray sum equals k with negatives?
questions.a: Prefix sums with a hash map counting earlier prefixes equal to current - k. O(n).

questions.q: Merge k sorted lists?
questions.a: A min-heap of the current heads, popping the smallest and pushing its successor. O(N log k).

questions.q: Find the median of two sorted arrays in O(log(min(m, n)))?
questions.a: Binary search the partition of the smaller array so that left halves are all <= right halves.

questions.q: Trapping rain water?
questions.a: Water above each bar is min(left max, right max) - height. Two pointers do it in O(n) and O(1) space.

questions.q: Longest substring without repeating characters?
questions.a: Sliding window with a map of last seen indexes; move the left edge past the previous occurrence.

questions.q: Group anagrams?
questions.a: Key each word by its sorted letters (or a 26-count tuple) in a hash map.

questions.q: Number of islands?
questions.a: Flood fill with DFS/BFS or union-find over the grid; count the components of land.

questions.q: Lowest common ancestor of a binary tree?
questions.a: Recurse; return the node if it matches, and the current node is the LCA when both subtrees report a hit.

questions.q: Serialise and deserialise a binary tree?
questions.a: Pre-order with null markers (or level order), parsed with the same order; unambiguous because nulls mark every missing child.

questions.q: Design an LRU cache.
questions.a: A hash map to doubly linked list nodes (or OrderedDict) giving O(1) get and put, evicting from the tail.

questions.q: Largest rectangle in a histogram?
questions.a: Monotonic stack of increasing heights; when a shorter bar arrives, pop and compute the area using the popped bar as the minimum. O(n).

questions.q: Word ladder shortest transformation?
questions.a: BFS over words differing by one letter, using wildcard buckets or letter substitution to generate neighbours.

questions.q: Course schedule feasibility?
questions.a: Topological sort: Kahn's algorithm processes all nodes iff there is no cycle.

questions.q: Kth largest element in an array?
questions.a: Quickselect in O(n) expected, or a min-heap of size k in O(n log k).

questions.q: How do you present a solution in an interview?
questions.a: Clarify the input and constraints, give a brute force, state complexity, optimise by naming the pattern, code cleanly, test with small and edge cases, then restate the complexity.

questions.q: How do you compute depth, parent and subtree size for every node?
questions.a: One DFS from the root (iterative for deep trees) records parent and depth; subtree sizes accumulate from children to parents in reverse visit order.

questions.q: What is the lowest common ancestor?
questions.a: The deepest node that is an ancestor of both given nodes. The tree distance between u and v is depth[u] + depth[v] - 2 depth[lca].

questions.q: Explain binary lifting.
questions.a: Precompute up[k][v], the 2^k-th ancestor of v. For LCA, lift the deeper node to equal depth using the bits of the difference, then lift both while their 2^k ancestors differ, and return the parent. O(n log n) preprocessing, O(log n) per query.

questions.q: How does an Euler tour turn subtree queries into range queries?
questions.a: Record entry and exit times in DFS. A subtree occupies the contiguous range [tin, tout), so subtree sums with point updates use a Fenwick tree in O(log n).

questions.q: How do you test whether u is an ancestor of v?
questions.a: tin[u] <= tin[v] < tout[u] using entry and exit times.

questions.q: How do you find the diameter of a tree?
questions.a: BFS from any node to the farthest node a, then BFS from a; the farthest distance is the diameter. It works for non-negative edge weights.

questions.q: What is a tree centre?
questions.a: The middle node (or two nodes) of a diameter path; rooting there minimises the height.

questions.q: Explain rerooting dynamic programming.
questions.a: Compute answers for the root in a bottom-up pass, then derive each child's answer from its parent's in a top-down pass, solving 'for every root' queries in O(n), such as the sum of distances.

questions.q: Give the rerooting recurrence for the sum of distances.
questions.a: ans[child] = ans[parent] - size[child] + (n - size[child]): nodes in the child's subtree get one closer and all others one farther.

questions.q: What is heavy-light decomposition and its complexity?
questions.a: It splits the tree into heavy chains by choosing the largest-subtree child at each node. A path crosses O(log n) light edges, so path queries with a segment tree cost O(log^2 n).

questions.q: Why does a path touch only O(log n) light edges?
questions.a: Each light edge leads to a subtree at most half the size of its parent's, so the subtree size at least doubles going up, limiting light edges to log n.

questions.q: What is a treap and why is it balanced?
questions.a: A BST by key and a heap by random priority. The random priorities make its shape equal to a random-insertion BST, giving expected O(log n) height with simple split and merge operations.

questions.q: How would you support 'k-th smallest' in a dynamic set?
questions.a: A balanced BST or treap with subtree sizes (order-statistic tree), or a Fenwick tree over compressed values with binary descent.

questions.q: What is the offline Tarjan LCA algorithm?
questions.a: A DFS using union-find that answers all LCA queries in near-linear time when they are known in advance.

questions.q: When do you binary search on the answer?
questions.a: When feasibility is monotone: if value x works then every larger (or smaller) value works, and a simple greedy check decides feasibility.

questions.q: Give three problems solved by binary search on the answer.
questions.a: Minimum eating speed, shipping capacity within D days, and split array largest sum (also aggressive cows, painter's partition).

questions.q: Explain sqrt decomposition.
questions.a: Split the array into blocks of about sqrt(n) with a summary each; queries combine whole-block summaries and partial ends in O(sqrt n), and updates fix a block summary.

questions.q: What is Mo's algorithm and its complexity?
questions.a: An offline method that sorts range queries by block of l then r, moving a window with O(1) add and remove, giving O((n + q) sqrt n) total pointer moves.

questions.q: How does divide and conquer count inversions?
questions.a: Merge sort; when merging, each time an element from the right half is placed before the remaining left elements it forms that many inversions. O(n log n).

questions.q: What is meet in the middle and when is it used?
questions.a: Split a 2^n search into two halves of 2^(n/2), enumerate both, and combine by sorting and binary search or hashing. It suits n around 30 to 40, such as subset sum and 4-sum variants.

questions.q: How do you iterate all submasks of a mask?
questions.a: sub = (sub - 1) & mask, starting from mask until sub becomes 0, visiting 2^popcount submasks.

questions.q: How does XOR find the single non-duplicated element?
questions.a: XOR of all elements cancels pairs (a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a), leaving the unique value.

questions.q: Exactly k distinct in a subarray count: how?
questions.a: atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1) with a sliding window and frequency map, O(n).

questions.q: How do you find two unique numbers when all others appear twice?
questions.a: XOR everything to get a ^ b, isolate a differing bit with x & -x, partition numbers by that bit and XOR each group.

questions.q: What is reservoir sampling?
questions.a: A one-pass method to sample k items uniformly from a stream of unknown length: keep the first k, then replace a random slot with probability k/(i+1) for item i.

questions.q: Monte Carlo versus Las Vegas algorithms?
questions.a: Monte Carlo has bounded running time but may be wrong with small probability; Las Vegas is always correct with random running time, such as randomised quicksort.

questions.q: What is Freivalds' algorithm?
questions.a: It verifies a matrix product A x B = C in O(n^2) with high probability by testing on random 0/1 vectors.

questions.q: Why randomise the pivot in quicksort or quickselect?
questions.a: It makes the expected running time O(n log n) or O(n) regardless of input order, defeating adversarial worst cases.

questions.q: How do you choose between a segment tree, sqrt decomposition and Mo's algorithm?
questions.a: Segment tree for associative operations with updates, sqrt decomposition for awkward merges with updates, Mo's for offline queries with cheap add and remove and no updates.

questions.q: What does the cross product of two vectors tell you?
questions.a: Its sign gives the orientation of the turn (counter-clockwise, clockwise or collinear) and its magnitude is twice the triangle area.

questions.q: Why avoid floating point in geometry?
questions.a: Rounding breaks equality, collinearity and orientation tests. Use integer arithmetic (cross products, squared distances) or exact fractions when possible.

questions.q: How do you test whether two segments intersect?
questions.a: Check that the endpoints of each segment lie on opposite sides of the other's line using orientation signs, with special handling of collinear and touching cases via bounding boxes.

questions.q: Describe ray casting for point in polygon.
questions.a: Count crossings of a horizontal ray from the point with the polygon's edges using a half-open rule; odd means inside.

questions.q: Explain Andrew's monotone chain for the convex hull.
questions.a: Sort points, build lower and upper hulls by popping the last point while the last three do not turn left, then join them. O(n log n).

questions.q: How do you compute polygon area?
questions.a: The shoelace formula: half the absolute sum of cross products of consecutive vertices; use the doubled value to stay in integers.

questions.q: What is a sweep line?
questions.a: A technique that processes sorted events while maintaining a structure of active objects, reducing 2D problems to 1D: interval overlaps, skyline, closest pair and segment intersection.

questions.q: State Bouton's theorem for Nim.
questions.a: A Nim position is losing for the player to move exactly when the XOR of the pile sizes is zero; from a nonzero XOR a move to zero exists.

questions.q: Explain the Sprague-Grundy theorem.
questions.a: Every impartial game position has a Grundy number equal to the mex of its options' numbers, and a sum of games has the XOR of its components' numbers; zero means the mover loses.

questions.q: How do you solve an unfamiliar impartial game?
questions.a: Define moves, compute Grundy numbers of one component by DP (often patterns appear), XOR the components, and a nonzero result means the first player wins.

questions.q: Describe minimax and alpha-beta pruning.
questions.a: Minimax values positions under optimal play; alpha-beta keeps bounds on what each side can guarantee and prunes branches that cannot change the result, giving big savings with good move ordering.

questions.q: How does the closest pair of points algorithm run in O(n log n)?
questions.a: Divide by x, solve halves, then check the strip of points within distance d of the dividing line sorted by y, where each point needs comparing with only a constant number of neighbours.

questions.q: What is Monte Carlo tree search?
questions.a: A game-tree search that uses random simulations to estimate move quality, balancing exploration and exploitation (UCT); effective for huge branching factors such as Go.

questions.q: How do you find the farthest pair of points?
questions.a: Compute the convex hull, then use rotating calipers to scan antipodal pairs in O(n) after the hull.

questions.q: How do you implement a hit counter for the last 5 minutes?
questions.a: A queue of timestamps removing expired entries on each call (amortised O(1)), or a circular array of per-second buckets for constant memory.

questions.q: How does a min stack return the minimum in O(1)?
questions.a: Store the minimum so far with each element, or keep a parallel stack of minima.

questions.q: Compare fixed window, sliding log and token bucket limiters.
questions.a: Fixed window is cheap but allows double the limit at boundaries; sliding log is exact but uses memory per request; token bucket uses O(1) state and allows bursts up to its capacity.

questions.q: Design a time-based key-value store.
questions.a: Per key, keep timestamps and values in lists as they arrive and answer get(key, t) with bisect_right on timestamps.

questions.q: How do you make tic-tac-toe moves O(1)?
questions.a: Keep counters for each row, column and both diagonals, adding +1 or -1 per player, and detect a win when a counter reaches n in absolute value.

questions.q: Which structures implement the snake game?
questions.a: A deque for the body and a set of occupied cells for O(1) collision checks; remove the tail before checking collisions on non-eating moves.

questions.q: How would you design an in-memory file system?
questions.a: A trie of path components where each node has children and optional file content, supporting mkdir, ls, add and read in O(path length).

questions.q: How do you design an iterator over nested lists?
questions.a: Keep a stack of iterators and advance lazily in has_next until the next integer is found, handling empty lists.

questions.q: Design an autocomplete system.
questions.a: A trie where each prefix node keeps sentence counts; top-3 by frequency then lexicographic order via a heap, with the completed sentence added on the terminator.

questions.q: How do you build a thread-safe bounded blocking queue?
questions.a: A lock with not-full and not-empty condition variables; put and get wait in while loops and notify the other condition.

questions.q: Design an event emitter with once and unsubscribe.
questions.a: A map from event to handler list; on returns an unsubscribe function; once wraps the handler to remove itself; emit iterates over a copy of the list.

questions.q: How do you implement an LRU cache with O(1) operations?
questions.a: A hash map plus a doubly linked list (or OrderedDict) moving accessed items to the front and evicting from the tail.

questions.q: How would you design a rate limiter that works across many servers?
questions.a: A shared store (Redis) with atomic token bucket or sliding window counters via Lua scripts, with local approximations to reduce round trips and a fail-open or fail-closed policy.

questions.q: What do you state when presenting a design class?
questions.a: The API, complexity of each operation, invariants, edge cases, concurrency assumptions and memory growth.

questions.q: Explain an array and a linked list with analogies.
questions.a: An array is a row of numbered lockers with instant access but costly insertion in the middle; a linked list is a treasure hunt where each clue points to the next, cheap to splice but slow to reach the n-th item.

questions.q: Explain a stack and a queue.
questions.a: A stack is a pile of plates (last in, first out); a queue is a line at a bank (first in, first out).

questions.q: Explain a hash table simply.
questions.a: A coat check: a computed ticket number tells you which hook to use, so lookup does not scan everything; collisions share a hook.

questions.q: Explain binary search with a game.
questions.a: Guess a number from 1 to 1000 with higher or lower hints: always guess the middle, halving the range each time, so about 10 guesses suffice.

questions.q: Explain BFS versus DFS with a picture.
questions.a: BFS is ripples in a pond finding the fewest hops; DFS is a mouse following one corridor to the end before backtracking.

questions.q: Explain a heap with an analogy.
questions.a: A tournament bracket where the winner sits on top; removing the winner replays a short chain of matches, so insert and remove are O(log n) while only the top is ordered.

questions.q: Explain dynamic programming simply.
questions.a: Remember answers to small subproblems so you never solve the same one twice, either by memoising recursion or by filling a table from small to large.

questions.q: When does greedy fail?
questions.a: When a locally best choice can prevent a better global result, as in coins 1, 3, 4 for amount 6 where 4 + 1 + 1 is worse than 3 + 3. Greedy needs a proof.

questions.q: Explain backtracking.
questions.a: Choose an option, explore, and undo the choice if it leads nowhere, like retreating to the last junction in a maze; pruning avoids hopeless branches.

questions.q: Explain union-find with an analogy.
questions.a: Friend groups at a party where each group has a leader: finding a person's group follows leaders upward, and merging groups links leaders, with path compression keeping chains short.

questions.q: Explain Dijkstra's idea.
questions.a: A rumour spreading proportionally to road lengths: the first time a town hears it gives the shortest distance, provided no road has negative length.

questions.q: How do you decide the complexity you need from the constraints?
questions.a: About 10^8 simple operations per second: n up to 20 allows 2^n, up to 500 allows n^3, up to 5,000 allows n^2, up to 10^6 needs n log n or n, and up to 10^9 needs log n or a formula.

questions.q: How do you recognise a DP problem?
questions.a: Counting or optimising with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, where a recursive brute force repeats the same states.

questions.q: What question separates stack-based from queue-based problems?
questions.a: Stacks handle most-recent-first problems like matching brackets, undo and next-greater; queues handle in-order or level-by-level problems like BFS and scheduling.
